questions.q: Priya says, 'Agriculture gives 46 per cent of India's GDP, because 46 per cent of workers depend on it.' Do you agree? Explain with the two figures from the chapter.
questions.a: No. About 46 per cent is the share of workers, while the share of GDP is a little over 18 per cent. The figures measure different things: how many people depend on it, and how much value it produces.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Gives 46 per cent for workers and a little over 18 per cent for GDP
Explains that the two measure people and output, so one cannot be read as the other

questions.q: A panchayat register lists six earners: (i) a hemp grower, (ii) a beekeeper who sells honey, (iii) a fish-pond owner, (iv) a tractor-repair garage owner, (v) a silkworm rearer who sells cocoons, (vi) a grocery shopkeeper. How many of the six fall under the Government of India's 'agriculture and allied activities' as the chapter lists them?
questions.a: The chapter's list covers fibre production such as hemp, beekeeping, fisheries, and rearing of silkworms. Repairing tractors and keeping a shop are services, not on the list. The wrong options add the garage or drop activities the list names.
o: Four: the hemp grower, beekeeper, fish-pond owner and silkworm rearer
Five: the four above and the tractor-repair garage, as it serves farming
Three: the hemp grower, fish-pond owner and silkworm rearer, as bees are not farmed
Two: the hemp grower and fish-pond owner, as only plants and fish are reared

questions.q: The Nair family's yearly income is: paddy ₹1,00,000; milk from two buffaloes ₹60,000; honey from beehives ₹20,000; sale of fish from a pond ₹20,000; the son's bank salary ₹1,00,000. A scheme officer says, 'Count only crop growing and this family is 33 per cent agricultural.' Using the chapter's meaning of 'agriculture and allied activities', work out the family's farm-linked share and explain why the officer's count gives a poor picture.
questions.a: Narrow count: only paddy, ₹1,00,000 of ₹3,00,000 = 33 per cent (one-third). Under the government's grouping, livestock (buffalo milk), beekeeping and fisheries are also counted, so the farm-linked income is 1,00,000 + 60,000 + 20,000 + 20,000 = ₹2,00,000, which is 67 per cent (two-thirds). The bank salary is not part of it. A crop-only count would show the family as one-third farming when two-thirds of its income comes from agriculture and allied activities, so it would understate how much rural families depend on the land.
s: Narrow count: paddy alone = ₹1,00,000 of ₹3,00,000, about 33 per cent
Names the allied activities in the family (livestock, beekeeping, fisheries) as counted by the government
Broad total ₹2,00,000 and share about 67 per cent, excluding the salary
Concludes that counting crops alone understates dependence on agriculture and allied activities

questions.q: Gurmeet argues, 'If the seed is good, any crop will grow equally well in any part of India.' Which set of factors from the chapter's opening discussion of crops and places best shows what is missing from his argument?
questions.a: The chapter says growing crops depends on several factors, such as soil, climate, the availability of water and the terrain, so the story of farming is linked to them. The wrong options list things a farm or community has, not the natural conditions the chapter names.
o: Soil, climate, availability of water and terrain, which differ by region
Seed company, tractor and size of the field, which differ from farm to farm
Language, religion and food habits of the people, which differ from state to state
Price of grain, number of workers and the time of the harvest festival

questions.q: Out of every 1,000 workers in India in 2022-23, about how many depended on agriculture and allied activities, and what share of every ₹1,000 of the country's output did these activities supply?
questions.a: 46 per cent of 1,000 is 460 workers, and a little over 18 per cent of ₹1,000 is a little over ₹180. The wrong options swap the two figures, repeat one figure for both, or borrow the 75 per cent figure that is about women.
o: About 460 workers; just over ₹180
About 180 workers; a little over ₹460
About 460 workers; about ₹460
About 750 workers; a little over ₹180

questions.q: Take the chapter's 2022-23 shares for a country of 100 workers and ₹100 of output: 46 workers depend on agriculture and allied activities, which give a little over ₹18; the other 54 workers produce the rest. (a) Work out the output per worker in each group. (b) What does the comparison suggest about how the value produced is spread over the workers?
questions.a: (a) Agriculture and allied activities: 18 / 46 = about ₹0.39 per worker. The rest: 82 / 54 = about ₹1.52 per worker. (b) A worker outside agriculture produces roughly four times as much as one in it, so many workers share a smaller share of the output; this is a calculation from the two figures, not a statement about effort.
s: (a) about ₹0.39 and about ₹1.52 per worker
(b) many workers share a smaller part of output, so output per worker is about four times lower in agriculture

questions.q: A seed company's advertisement shows only men driving tractors and says, 'The Indian farmer: strong, male, mechanised.' Using the chapter, (a) give the figure that shows the advertisement leaves out most of the workers, (b) name two farm operations the chapter says women perform, and (c) say whether the tractor in the picture is enough to describe India's farming.
questions.a: (a) In rural India more than 75 per cent of people working in agriculture are women (2025). (b) Women perform most operations, from sowing to harvesting and threshing. (c) No: the chapter describes farming as a blend of traditional and modern, and Fig. 1.1 shows oxen ploughing and women transplanting by hand as well as a tractor and a transplanter.
s: (a) more than 75 per cent of rural agricultural workers are women
(b) two operations from sowing, harvesting, threshing
(c) the tractor shows only the modern side; farming is a blend of traditional and modern practices

questions.q: Describe, in three or four lines, a farm family that is NOT only a crop-growing family but still comes under 'agriculture and allied activities'. Name three different activities and the broad head (farming, animal husbandry, forestry or horticulture) under which each falls.
questions.a: Any valid family, e.g. it grows paddy (farming), keeps cows (animal husbandry) and grows mango trees (horticulture). Fish rearing or silk cocoons may be added as allied activities.
s: Names three different activities
Places at least two under the correct broad head
Description is coherent and stays within the chapter's list

questions.q: A taluka has 8,000 working people. If it matched India's 2022-23 share, about ___ of them would depend on agriculture and allied activities.

A tourism poster titled 'Incredible Agricultural India' shows only a Punjab wheat field with a tractor and a male farmer. Evaluate whether the poster fairly represents the agricultural landscape described in the chapter. In your answer name regions and crops the poster misses, say what in the chapter's Fig. 1.1 shows the poster misses, and say which group of workers it overlooks.
questions.a: The poster shows one region and one machine. The chapter names saffron in the Kashmir valley, tea in the Northeast and the Nilgiris, and paddy in Kerala as well as wheat in Punjab. Fig. 1.1 shows oxen-drawn ploughing and women transplanting rice by hand beside the tractor and the transplanter, so the landscape is a blend of traditional and modern practices. The poster also overlooks women, who are more than 75 per cent of those working in agriculture in rural India. Verdict: it is a one-sided picture.
s: At least two other regions with their crops (Kashmir saffron, Northeast or Nilgiris tea, Kerala paddy)
Traditional practices from Fig. 1.1 beside the tractor, so it is a blend
Overlooks women, more than 75 per cent of agricultural workers in rural India
A reasoned verdict that the poster is one-sided

questions.q: A survey team plans to interview 200 people who work in agriculture in rural India. Going by the chapter's figure for women, at least how many of the 200 should the team expect to be women?
questions.a: More than 75 per cent of rural agricultural workers are women, and 75 per cent of 200 is 150. Half (100) ignores the figure, 92 applies the 46 per cent workers share by mistake, and 36 applies the 18 per cent GDP share.
o: Above 150
About 100 women
About 92 women
About 36 women

questions.q: Nisha runs a self-help group of 50 members: 20 grow crops, 18 rear goats and 12 farm fish. She says, 'Agri means field, so only the 20 of us growing crops are in agriculture.' (a) Correct her, using the Government of India's grouping in the chapter. (b) What share of her group would a crop-only count have left out?
questions.a: (a) The government classifies agriculture and allied activities broadly, including livestock-related work and fisheries, so the goat rearers and fish farmers are inside it. (b) 18 + 12 = 30 of 50 members = 60 per cent would be left out.
s: (a) livestock rearing and fisheries are counted in the government's broad grouping
(b) 30 of 50 = 60 per cent

questions.q: True or False: Because 'agri' means field, a family that only keeps bees and sells honey is outside agriculture in the sense the chapter uses.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Government of India counts beekeeping (apiculture) under 'agriculture and allied activities', so a bee-keeping family is inside agriculture in this broad sense; 'agri' describes the word's Latin origin, not the limit of the activities.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: beekeeping is listed with agriculture and allied activities; word origin does not limit the meaning

questions.q:
Assertion (A): About 46 per cent of India's working population depends on agriculture and allied activities.
Reason (R): A little over 18 per cent of India's GDP comes from agriculture and allied activities.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the 18 per cent GDP share measures value produced, not the number of workers, so it does not explain why 46 per cent of workers depend on farming.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Fig. 1.1 of the chapter shows two ways of doing the same jobs: ploughing with a ploughshare pulled by oxen and with a tractor, and transplanting rice seedlings by women's hands and with a transplanter. (a) Name the two jobs and say which method for each is the older. (b) A farmer ploughs his small plot with bullocks but hires a tractor for his big field. Which statement of the chapter does his practice illustrate?
questions.a: (a) Ploughing (oxen older, tractor newer) and transplanting seedlings (by hand older, transplanter newer). (b) Many farmers use a combination of traditional and modern methods.
s: (a) ploughing and transplanting, with oxen and hand as the older methods
(b) many farmers use a combination of methods

questions.q:
Students of Class 7 at a school in Nashik surveyed the 600 working people of Dhanori village. Crop farming: 210. Livestock rearing: 30. Beekeeping: 12. Fish farming: 8. Silk cocoon rearing: 10. Other work (shops, school, transport): 330. Of the workers whose main work is crop farming, livestock rearing, beekeeping, fish farming or cocoon rearing, 216 are women.
(a) Which entries does the government count under 'agriculture and allied activities', and how many workers do they add up to?
(b) What per cent of the village workers is this group, and how does it compare with the national figure in the chapter?
(c) What per cent of the group are women, and does it fit the chapter's statement about rural India?
(d) The gram panchayat can fund only one training day: for the 210 crop growers, or for all workers in the group. Which would you recommend, and why?
questions.a: (a) All five farm-linked entries: crop farming, livestock, beekeeping, fish farming and silk cocoon rearing; not 'other work'. (b) 270 of 600 = 45 per cent, close to the national figure of about 46 per cent. (c) 216 of 270 = 80 per cent, which is more than 75 per cent, so it fits. (d) A defended choice: the crop-growers-only day reaches 210 of the 270 (about 78 per cent) with one focus; the wider day reaches all 270, including the allied workers and the women who are 80 per cent of the group.
s: Part (a): crop, livestock, beekeeping, fish and cocoon entries counted (270 workers), other work excluded
Part (b): 45 per cent, close to about 46 per cent nationally
Part (c): 80 per cent, above the 75 per cent in the chapter
Part (d): a recommendation supported by the figures (210 of 270 or all 270, 80 per cent women)

questions.q: Block A has 5,000 working people, of whom 2,300 depend on agriculture and allied activities. Block B has 4,000 working people, of whom 1,900 do. (a) Work out the share in each block. (b) Which block is closer to the national share the chapter gives for 2022-23, and by how many percentage points does the other differ?
questions.a: (a) Block A: 2,300 / 5,000 = 46 per cent. Block B: 1,900 / 4,000 = 47.5 per cent. (b) Block A matches the national 46 per cent exactly; Block B is 1.5 percentage points above it.
s: (a) 46 per cent and 47.5 per cent
(b) Block A matches 46 per cent; Block B is 1.5 percentage points higher

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Threshing means removing the edible grain from the straw or husk, by hand or by machine.
2. The figure of about 46 per cent means that 46 per cent of India's goods and services come from agriculture and allied activities.
3. The word agriculture also takes in animal husbandry, forestry and horticulture.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are from the chapter. 2 is false: 46 per cent is the share of the working population; the share of goods and services produced is a little over 18 per cent.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Sundarpur block has 10,000 working people and produces goods and services worth ₹200 crore a year. A block officer notes the two national figures for 2022-23 from the chapter: about 46 per cent and a little over 18 per cent. The block has a training budget of ₹10 lakh. Imran proposes to divide it between agriculture and other work in the ratio of the 46 per cent figure; Zoya proposes the ratio of the 18 per cent figure.
(a) What does each of the two national figures measure?
(b) If Sundarpur matched both national shares, how many of its workers and how many ₹ crore of its output would belong to agriculture and allied activities?
(c) Compute the agriculture share of the budget under each proposal. Whose proposal follows the number of people who depend on farming?
(d) The block can fund only one training: beekeeping and fish rearing for farm families, or a course for crop growers only. Which fits the chapter's meaning of 'agriculture and allied activities' better, and why?
questions.a: (a) 46 per cent is the share of the working population; 18 per cent is the share of the value of goods and services produced (GDP). (b) 46 per cent of 10,000 = 4,600 workers; 18 per cent of ₹200 crore = ₹36 crore. (c) Imran: 46 per cent of ₹10 lakh = ₹4.6 lakh; Zoya: 18 per cent = ₹1.8 lakh. Imran's follows the number of people who depend on farming. (d) The allied-activities training is better supported: the chapter counts livestock, bees, fisheries and silk as part of agriculture, so many families earn from them; a crop-only course would reach only part of the group. A crop-only choice can be defended if the reason uses the stem.
s: Part (a): 46 per cent is workers, 18 per cent is GDP
Part (b): 4,600 workers and ₹36 crore
Part (c): ₹4.6 lakh and ₹1.8 lakh; Imran's follows the headcount
Part (d): a choice with a reason that uses the chapter's meaning of allied activities

questions.q: A news channel quotes the chapter's two 2022-23 figures (about 46 per cent of workers, a little over 18 per cent of GDP) and draws four conclusions. Which conclusion goes BEYOND what the two figures can show?
questions.a: The figures give shares of workers and of output; they do not give anyone's earnings, and 18 per cent is a share of national output, not a ratio of incomes. The other three conclusions read the shares correctly.
o: Each farm worker earns only 18 per cent of what a worker outside farming earns
Nearly half of India's workers depend on agriculture and allied activities
A little under one-fifth of the country's output comes from agriculture and allied activities
A large share of workers shares a comparatively small part of the output

questions.q: In a village survey, 252 of the 360 people working in agriculture are women. (a) What per cent is that? (b) The chapter says more than 75 per cent of people working in agriculture in rural India are women. Does this village prove the chapter wrong? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 252 / 360 = 70 per cent. (b) No. The chapter's figure describes rural India as a whole (2025); one village can be above or below it, just as the share of workers in one block can differ from the national 46 per cent.
s: (a) 70 per cent
(b) the chapter's figure is for rural India as a whole, so one village below it does not contradict it

questions.q: A museum label reads: 'Rice farming was systematically practised in the Ganga Plain in the 7th or 8th millennium BCE, because rice grains were found there.' How does the chapter treat this claim?
questions.a: The chapter reports rice grains in the Ganga Plain as early as the 7th or 8th millennium BCE, but adds that some experts say this need not mean systematic cultivation, which may have taken a few more millennia. The wrong options overclaim, deny the finding, or move it to barley.
o: Grains were found, but cultivation need not be systematic
The claim is proved, since any grain find shows systematic farming
The claim is wrong, since rice reached India only with the Harappans
The claim is right for barley, but no rice grain of that age exists

questions.q: A student writes in a project: 'No farming practice recorded in the distant past is still followed today; it was all given up long ago.' Show, with two examples from the chapter, that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The Brihatsamhita describes a method of grafting that the chapter says is still in use today. The Kalibangan furrows show intercropping around 2800 BCE, and the same practice was seen again in the 1960s. Two practices that survive from ancient times contradict the claim.
s: Grafting method in the Brihatsamhita is still in use today
Intercropping at Kalibangan around 2800 BCE seen again in the 1960s
Concludes that these examples contradict the claim that nothing survives

questions.q: A farmer's seed box holds cotton, hemp, mustard, jute, green gram, castor and mango stones. By the chapter's grouping of crops, the number of fibre crops in the box is ___.

A museum shows two photographs of fields in Rajasthan with the same pattern of perpendicular furrows: one from the Harappan site of Kalibangan, dated around 2800 BCE, and one from the 1960s. Which conclusion does the chapter support?
questions.a: The chapter's Fig. 1.2 shows intercropping at Kalibangan around 2800 BCE, evidenced by perpendicular furrows, and the same practice continuing in the 1960s. The wrong options reverse the order, assume a gap the caption does not mention, or read the furrows as machine work.
o: A farming practice, intercropping, continued for thousands of years
Intercropping was invented in the 1960s and copied back to Harappa
Intercropping was given up after the Harappan period and revived later
The furrows prove the Harappans ploughed with tractors

questions.q: A teacher says, 'The story of Indian farming begins only with the written texts.' Evaluate this using the chapter. Give two finds from before the texts with their millennia or dates, one piece of field evidence, and say what the chapter itself says about when the texts belong.
questions.a: The claim is not supported. The chapter says the story of Indian farming goes back to prehistory: rice grains in the Ganga Plain as early as the 7th or 8th millennium BCE (though systematic cultivation may have taken longer), and barley and millets at Mehrgarh in the 7th millennium BCE. Perpendicular furrows at Kalibangan show intercropping around 2800 BCE. The ancient texts, such as the Arthashastra and the Vrikshayurveda, are introduced as the information of the 'historical period', after these earlier finds. So texts record the later chapters of a much older story.
s: Two earlier finds with their dates (Ganga Plain rice; Mehrgarh barley and millets)
Kalibangan furrows as field evidence for intercropping around 2800 BCE
The chapter places the texts in the historical period, after prehistory
A reasoned verdict that the claim is not supported

questions.q: An orchard owner wants mango plants that are both sweet and pest-resistant without waiting for a new variety. Which method from the chapter serves her, and which text does the chapter say describes a form of it that is still in use?
questions.a: Grafting joins one plant with another to grow as a single plant and combine traits such as pest resistance or sweetness; the chapter says the Brihatsamhita describes a grafting method still in use today. The Vrikshayurveda is credited with seed preparation, soil and planting advice.
o: Grafting, described in Varahamihira's Brihatsamhita
Intercropping, described in Varahamihira's Brihatsamhita
Grafting, described in Surapala's Vrikshayurveda
Seed preparation, described in the Krishiparashara

questions.q:
Kavya's club audits her kitchen. The items are: sesame oil, black gram dal, wheat flour, a jute shopping bag, mango pickle and rice. The club wants a poster that says 'Everything in this kitchen was grown in Vedic times.' The chapter says the Vedas mention yava, godhuma, vrihi, sesame, black gram and various pulses and legumes.
(a) Name the group (oilseed, legume, fibre crop or fruit) for the sesame oil, black gram dal, jute bag and mango pickle.
(b) How many of the six items come from crops the Vedas are said to mention?
(c) Which items are missing from that list of Vedic mentions?
(d) The club has two draft posters. Draft A: 'Four of the six items in this kitchen come from crops the Vedas mention.' Draft B: 'Every item in this kitchen comes from a crop that the chapter says Indian farmers learned to grow over time.' Which draft would you print, and what must the poster not claim?
questions.a: (a) Sesame: oilseed; black gram: legume; jute: fibre crop; mango: fruit. (b) Four: sesame, black gram, wheat (godhuma) and rice (vrihi). (c) The jute bag and the mango pickle. (d) Both drafts are supported by the chapter: A is more exact about the Vedas, B covers all six items. Either can be chosen with a reason, but the poster must not say that all six items are Vedic, because the chapter does not say the Vedas mention jute or mango.
s: Part (a): oilseed, legume, fibre crop, fruit
Part (b): four of six
Part (c): jute and mango
Part (d): picks a draft with a reason and does not claim that all six items are Vedic

questions.q: Meera sows sugarcane and pumpkin together in one field in the same season. Imran grows mustard in a field, harvests it, and sows a pulse there in the next season. (a) Whose practice is intercropping, going by the chapter's definition? (b) What does the definition say that rules out the other farmer's practice?
questions.a: (a) Meera's. (b) Intercropping means growing two or more different crops simultaneously; Imran grows his crops one after another, not at the same time.
s: (a) Meera's practice is intercropping
(b) the definition requires crops to be grown simultaneously, which Imran's are not

questions.q: Surapala's Vrikshayurveda says: 'Newly planted trees in arid land should be watered every morning and evening for a period of fifteen days until the soil is fully soaked.' (a) Name two details of the practice that this advice fixes. (b) What does the chapter add about other types of soil, and what does this suggest about the text's knowledge?
questions.a: (a) Any two: watering twice a day (morning and evening), for fifteen days, until the soil is fully soaked, for newly planted trees. (b) The chapter says the text gives further recommendations on irrigation methods for other types of soils, which suggests the knowledge was detailed and matched watering to the kind of land.
s: (a) two details: time of day, fifteen days, newly planted trees, soaking the soil
(b) other soils have further irrigation recommendations
Concludes that the text matched its advice to the type of land

questions.q: Arjun says, 'Rice was the first and only grain the Harappans knew.' Is he right? Answer with evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Barley and wheat were the staple crops of the Harappans. Rice appears at several Harappan sites only in the 3rd millennium BCE and only in some regions, along with millets and several vegetables. So rice was neither first nor the only grain.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Barley and wheat were the staples
Rice was present only in some regions, with millets and vegetables as well

questions.q: A quiz-writer lists four things connected with farming in the chapter. Which one is NOT attributed by the chapter to a named ancient text?
questions.a: The chapter attributes grafting to the Brihatsamhita, the dew-soaking of cereals and pulses to the Arthashastra, and sections on land preparation and payment to farmers to the Arthashastra. Bamboo drip irrigation is described as a traditional system practised in parts of northeastern India, not tied to a text.
o: Bamboo pipes bringing spring water to fields in the northeast
A method of grafting that is still in use
Instructions on preparing seeds, such as soaking cereals and pulses in dew
Sections on preparing land and on payment to farmers

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Rice grains of the 7th or 8th millennium BCE in the Ganga Plain prove that systematic rice cultivation had already been mastered.
2. Barley and wheat were the staple crops of the Harappans.
3. Cattle, sheep, goats and other animals were domesticated from the pre-urban phase of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation, about 3500 BCE.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 follow the chapter. 1 is false: the chapter says experts point out that the grains need not mean cultivation was systematic, which may have taken a few more millennia.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rice was present at several Harappan sites in the 3rd millennium BCE, at least in some regions.
Reason (R): Barley and wheat were the staple crops of the Harappans.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true. The staples being barley and wheat does not explain why rice appears at some sites, so R is not the explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match the practice in Column A with the source the chapter links it to in Column B.
Column A: 1. Seeds sprinkled with milk, rubbed with cow dung and smeared with honey and false black pepper  2. Cotton seeds smeared with cow dung, and cereals and pulses soaked in dew  3. A method of joining two plants to grow as one  4. The names yava, godhuma and vrihi for barley, wheat and rice
Column B: a. Brihatsamhita  b. Vedas  c. Vrikshayurveda  d. Arthashastra
questions.a: Surapala's Vrikshayurveda gives the milk, cow dung, honey and false black pepper treatment; Kautilya's Arthashastra gives cotton seeds with cow dung and the dew-soaking of cereals and pulses; the Brihatsamhita describes grafting; the Vedas mention yava, godhuma and vrihi. The wrong options swap the two seed-preparation texts or the grafting and Vedas entries.

questions.q: True or False: Surapala's advice to water newly planted trees morning and evening for fifteen days is meant for trees planted in every kind of soil.
questions.a: False. The chapter quotes this advice for newly planted trees in arid land; it says further recommendations give irrigation methods for other types of soils.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: the quoted advice is for arid land, and other soils have other irrigation methods

questions.q: Ravi says, 'Surapala's Vrikshayurveda and Kautilya's Arthashastra give the same seed advice, because both use cow dung.' Evaluate his claim using what each text says about preparing seeds, and say what the difference shows about the knowledge in the texts.
questions.a: Ravi is partly right. Both use cow dung. But Surapala gives one treatment: seeds sprinkled with milk, rubbed with cow dung, dried and smeared with honey and false black pepper. The Arthashastra gives advice by crop: cotton seeds smeared with cow dung, cereals, beans and pulses soaked in dew for some days and sun-dried, and sugarcane smeared at the cut with honey, ghee and lard and covered with cow dung. So the advice is not the same. The difference shows that the texts hold detailed, crop-wise knowledge of how to prepare seeds.
s: Verdict: partly right, the common ingredient cow dung
Surapala's treatment with milk, honey and false black pepper
Arthashastra's crop-wise advice (cotton, cereals and pulses, or sugarcane)
States that the two are not the same advice
Inference: the texts hold detailed, crop-wise knowledge

questions.q: A village in a dry district plants 12 saplings and has water for only 300 waterings from its well during the first fifteen days. It follows Surapala's rule of watering every morning and evening. (a) Is 300 waterings enough for all 12 saplings for the full fifteen days? (b) For how many full days can all 12 be watered on this rule?
questions.a: (a) Each sapling needs 2 x 15 = 30 waterings, so 12 saplings need 360; 300 is 60 short. (b) 300 / (12 x 2) = 12.5, so all 12 can be watered for 12 full days.
s: (a) needs 360 waterings, so 300 is not enough (60 short)

questions.q:
At the school's heritage fair, a stall shows three unlabelled cards. Card X: 'Seeds sprinkled with milk, rubbed with cow dung, dried and smeared with honey and false black pepper definitely sprout.' Card Y: 'Cotton seeds are smeared with cow dung; cereals, beans and pulses are soaked in dew for some days and sun-dried before planting.' Card Z: 'Newly planted trees in arid land should be watered every morning and evening for fifteen days.' Each card must be labelled either Surapala's Vrikshayurveda or Kautilya's Arthashastra.
(a) Give the correct label for each card.
(b) A visitor wants to use Card Z for a tree in a different kind of soil. What does the chapter say about this?
(c) What kinds of knowledge do the cards together show?
(d) The sponsor offers two headlines: 'Ancient texts gave exact, crop-wise instructions' or 'Ancient texts gave only general advice'. Which do the cards support better, and why?
questions.a: (a) X: Vrikshayurveda; Y: Arthashastra; Z: Vrikshayurveda. (b) Card Z is advice for newly planted trees in arid land; the chapter says the text gives further recommendations for irrigation methods for other types of soils. (c) Practical knowledge of preparing seeds (with milk, dung, honey, dew) and of watering trees. (d) The first headline: Card Y gives separate treatments for cotton, cereals and pulses, and Card Z gives a fixed schedule of mornings and evenings for fifteen days.
s: Part (a): X Vrikshayurveda, Y Arthashastra, Z Vrikshayurveda
Part (b): Card Z is for arid land; other soils have other irrigation recommendations
Part (c): seed preparation and watering of trees, practical knowledge
Part (d): first headline, supported by crop-wise treatments or the fixed schedule

questions.q: (a) Which grain does the chapter name both for Mehrgarh in the 7th millennium BCE and among the staple crops of the Harappans? (b) Wheat is named among the Harappan staples but not for Mehrgarh. Does that prove wheat was unknown at Mehrgarh? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Barley. (b) No. The chapter does not mention wheat at Mehrgarh, but not mentioning a crop is not evidence that it was absent.
s: (a) barley
(b) no; the chapter is silent about wheat at Mehrgarh, which does not show it was unknown

questions.q: A student arranges four finds from the chapter in time. Which arrangement is right?
questions.a: Rice grains in the Ganga Plain go back to the 7th or 8th millennium BCE, animal domestication to about 3500 BCE, and rice at some Harappan sites to the 3rd millennium BCE. The wrong options reverse the order.
o: Ganga Plain rice, then animal domestication about 3500 BCE, then rice at some Harappan sites
Animal domestication about 3500 BCE, then rice grains in the Ganga Plain, then rice at some Harappan sites
Rice at some Harappan sites, then rice grains in the Ganga Plain, then animal domestication about 3500 BCE
Rice at some Harappan sites, then animal domestication about 3500 BCE, then rice grains in the Ganga Plain

questions.q: The chapter's Fig. 1.2 compares intercropping at Kalibangan around 2800 BCE with the same practice in the 1960s. (a) A student works out the gap as 2800 - 1960 = 840 years. What mistake has she made? (b) Give the correct gap and say what the chapter rounds it to.
questions.a: (a) She subtracted, but 2800 BCE lies before the year 1 and 1960 CE lies after it, so the years on the two sides of the calendar's zero must be added. (b) 2800 + 1960 = 4,760 years, which the chapter rounds to around 4,800 years.
s: (a) BCE and CE years lie on opposite sides of the year 1, so they are added, not subtracted
(b) 4,760 years, rounded to about 4,800 in the chapter

questions.q:
Lakshmi, a farmer in Andhra Pradesh, keeps a diary. Rice crop 1 is sown in June. Rice crop 2 is sown in October. Rice crop 3 is sown in February, a dry month. Her cousin Mohan in a north Indian village grows only a monsoon crop and leaves his field idle in the dry months.
(a) Which rain or water source supports each of the three crops?
(b) Name two sources, other than rain, from which a farmer could irrigate crop 3, and say which of them the chapter says is fast decreasing in many parts of India.
(c) Which water sources could Mohan use in the dry months if he wanted to sow a crop?
(d) This year the water level in Lakshmi's well has fallen. Should she keep the third rice crop or leave the field idle or switch to a less thirsty crop in those months? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Crop 1: southwest monsoon (June to September); crop 2: northeast monsoon (October to December); crop 3: irrigation. (b) Any two of groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds; groundwater is the source that is fast decreasing. (c) Groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds or moisture retained in the soil. (d) A choice with a reason: keeping the crop uses irrigation to farm all year, as Andhra Pradesh does, but the chapter says groundwater reserves are fast decreasing in many parts of India, so leaving the field idle or choosing a less thirsty crop protects the water.
s: Part (a): southwest monsoon, northeast monsoon, irrigation
Part (b): two irrigation sources and groundwater as the one fast decreasing
Part (c): two dry-season sources for Mohan
Part (d): a decision tied to irrigation against falling groundwater

questions.q: True or False: India's 15 agroclimatic zones are the same thing as the seven climate types, only counted differently.
questions.a: False. The chapter treats them as different: the seven climate types describe climate, while the 15 agroclimatic zones combine climate factors with types of soil and terrain and types of vegetation.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: the zones combine climate, soil, terrain and vegetation, which the seven climate types do not

questions.q: A column in a farm magazine says, 'Farming in India depends on the monsoon alone.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter: refer to the two monsoons and the regions they water, to what farmers in north India do in the dry period, and to the states that grow rice all year.
questions.a: The claim is only partly true. The southwest monsoon (June to September) is crucial for kharif crops in northern and central India, and the northeast monsoon (October to December) brings rain to the east and south, with Malabar and Coromandel getting both. But in the dry period between the monsoons, farmers in north India rely on groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds and soil moisture. Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh grow rice throughout the year because of monsoon water as well as irrigation. So the monsoon is central, but irrigation and other sources also decide what is grown.
s: Southwest monsoon: months and its importance for kharif crops in the north and centre
Northeast monsoon: months and the east and south, with both on Malabar and Coromandel
Dry-period sources for north Indian farmers
All-year rice states depend on monsoon water as well as irrigation
Verdict: the monsoon is central but not the only factor

questions.q: An official report calls a district 'Western Dry Region'. Another report calls the same area 'arid'. A student says the two labels are just different names for one thing. Which reply is correct, going by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter gives Western Dry Region as an example of an agroclimatic zone (one of 15), made by combining climate factors with types of soil, terrain and vegetation. Arid is one of the seven climate types, which describe climate only.
o: No: 'Western Dry Region' is a zone built from climate, soil, terrain and vegetation; 'arid' is a climate type
No: 'Western Dry Region' is one of the seven climate types, and 'arid' is an agroclimatic zone
Yes: the 15 agroclimatic zones are simply the seven climate types under new names, so the labels agree
Yes: both labels describe only the amount of rain a place receives, so they are interchangeable

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Farmers on the Malabar and Coromandel plains can grow crops in the period between the two monsoons.
Reason (R): The northeast monsoon brings rain to every state of India, including the north.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: rain from both monsoons lets farmers in the south grow crops in between. R is false: the northeast monsoon brings rain to the east and south, and the in-between period is a dry season for north Indian farmers.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
An agricultural officer compares two villages with invented rainfall figures. Village P: 300 mm from June to September and 450 mm from October to December. Village Q: 800 mm from June to September and no rain from October to December. One village lies on the Coromandel plain and the other in the Upper Gangetic Plain.
(a) Which village is the Coromandel one, and why?
(b) What per cent of Village P's rain falls from October to December?
(c) Which village's farmers will need more irrigation water in October to December, and from what sources can they get it?
(d) The district can give a canal-water subsidy to only one village this year. Which would you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Village P: it gets a large share from the northeast monsoon (October to December), as the Coromandel plain does, while Q gets all of its rain in the southwest monsoon. (b) 450 of 750 = 60 per cent. (c) Village Q; groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds or soil moisture. (d) Two defensible answers: Q has no rain at all in its dry season, while P grows crops in between and may still need irrigation for rice in the lean months.
s: Part (a): P, because of heavy October to December rain from the northeast monsoon
Part (b): 60 per cent
Part (c): Q, with a source such as groundwater, canals, rivers or ponds
Part (d): a choice supported with the rainfall figures and the chapter's idea of a dry season

questions.q: The chapter asks what would happen if your state received less than normal monsoon rain for two consecutive years. Describe two effects on farming and one effect on the family meal, using the chapter's ideas.
questions.a: Kharif crops depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon, so they would fail or fall; farmers would need groundwater, rivers, canals or ponds; foods made from the affected crops, such as rice or pulses, could disappear from meals or become difficult to get.
s: First effect on farming
Second effect on farming or water use
An effect on food on the table, with a reason

questions.q: Suppose the northeast monsoon fails in a year. (a) Which farmer feels the loss first, one on the Coromandel plain or one in the Upper Gangetic Plain who grows only monsoon crops? (b) Give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) The farmer on the Coromandel plain. (b) The Coromandel plain receives rain from both monsoons and its farmers grow crops in between; the northeast monsoon rains on the east and south, so the northern farmer was not relying on it.
s: (a) Coromandel farmer
(b) the plain receives rain from both monsoons and the northeast monsoon rains on the east and south

questions.q: Xuanzang, a Chinese pilgrim of the 7th century, wrote that 'the climate and the quality of the soil being different according to situation, the produce of the land is various in its character.' (a) Which two factors did he name as the reasons for the variety of produce? (b) The chapter builds the agroclimatic zones from these and two further factors. Name them.
questions.a: (a) Climate and the quality of the soil. (b) Terrain and types of vegetation.
s: (a) climate and the quality of the soil
(b) terrain and vegetation

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Farmers in north India depend on the northeast monsoon for their crops in the dry season between the two monsoons.
Reason (R): In that season they use groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds and moisture retained in the soil.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the northeast monsoon rains on the east and south, and the in-between period is a dry season in the north. R is true, because those are the sources the chapter names for north Indian farmers.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: The northeast monsoon fails in a year. Which farmer's crop plan, as described by the chapter, is hit hardest?
questions.a: The northeast monsoon prevails from October to December and rains on the east and south, including the Coromandel plain. The kharif sowing in the north and centre relies on the southwest monsoon, and an idle field uses no rain.
o: A Coromandel farmer who sows a crop in the first week of November
A north Indian farmer who sows kharif crops with the June rains
A central Indian farmer who sows kharif crops with the first southwest monsoon showers
A north Indian farmer who leaves the field idle between the monsoons

questions.q: Rohan says, 'India has just one rainy season, from June to September, so a farmer anywhere in India can sow only once a year.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The northeast monsoon from October to December rains on the east and south, and the Malabar and Coromandel plains get both. Southern farmers grow crops in between, and Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh grow rice throughout the year with monsoon and irrigation.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Names the second, northeast monsoon and its months and regions
Gives the all-year rice example or the crops grown in between

questions.q: A scheme tells farmers across India: 'Sow every crop in the first week of June with the monsoon rains.' Show from the chapter that this single date cannot suit every region.
questions.a: The southwest monsoon rains from June to September and is crucial for kharif crops in northern and central India, so June sowing suits them. But on the Coromandel plain the northeast monsoon from October to December gives rain for an October crop, and in north India the dry period crops depend on groundwater, rivers, canals and ponds. One date cannot fit regions with different rain periods.
s: June sowing fits the southwest monsoon (June to September) for kharif crops in the north and centre
Coromandel gets northeast monsoon rain from October to December, so a crop there follows a different date
Concludes that regions with different rain periods and water sources need different dates

questions.q: A news report says, 'India has seven climate types and two monsoons, so no common rule for growing crops can exist and planning should be left to each farmer.' Evaluate this report. Use what the chapter says about the climate types, the monsoons and the agroclimatic zones.
questions.a: The report is partly right. The seven climate types differ in sunshine, rainfall and temperature, and the two monsoons affect regions differently, so one rule for the whole country would not work. But the chapter says India is divided into 15 agroclimatic zones that combine climate factors with types of soil and terrain and types of vegetation. This categorisation helps the government and other agencies plan what, when and how to grow different crops. So planning is possible region by region, not only farm by farm.
s: Climate types and monsoons differ across regions (partly right)
Gives sunshine, rainfall or temperature as differences between climate types
Agroclimatic zones combine climate, soil, terrain and vegetation
Zones help government and agencies plan what, when and how to grow
A balanced verdict: no single national rule, but planning by zones is possible

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. India is divided into 15 agroclimatic zones made by combining climate, soil, terrain and vegetation.
2. The northeast monsoon, from October to December, brings rain to the east and south of India.
3. Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh can grow rice only in the monsoon months because they have no irrigation.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are from the chapter. 3 is false: those states grow rice throughout the year because of monsoon water as well as irrigation.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: (a) Which climate type does the chapter give for the western coastal strip, and which for eastern India and the southern peninsula? (b) A student says both are 'wet' places, so the same crops will suit both. Why is this too hasty a conclusion?
questions.a: (a) Tropical wet for the western coastal strip; tropical for eastern India and the southern peninsula. (b) The chapter says each area receives different amounts of sunshine and rainfall, has different temperature changes across the seasons and is affected differently by the monsoons; the agroclimatic zones also bring in soil, terrain and vegetation.
s: (a) tropical wet for the western coastal strip; tropical for eastern India and the southern peninsula
(b) different sunshine, rainfall, temperature or monsoon effects, and soil, terrain and vegetation, so the same crops will not necessarily suit both

questions.q: Two farmers each sow a crop in the first week of November: one on the Malabar coast and one in the Upper Gangetic Plain. (a) Which farmer can count on rain for the crop? (b) From what sources can the other farmer get water?
questions.a: (a) The Malabar farmer: the northeast monsoon (October to December) rains there, as Malabar gets both monsoons. (b) The north Indian farmer: groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds or moisture retained in the soil.
s: (a) Malabar farmer, with the northeast monsoon from October to December
(b) two of groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds, soil moisture

questions.q: A rice variety needs 120 days. A farmer on the Coromandel plain sows it on 1 October, and the northeast monsoon rains end with December. The crop will need water from irrigation for the last ___ days.
Groundwater levels fall sharply in a district. Going by the chapter, which farmer is most exposed?
questions.a: North Indian farmers in the dry period depend on groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds and soil moisture to irrigate their crops. The other farmers are watered by monsoon rain or are not growing a crop at that time, so a fall in groundwater affects them least.
o: A north Indian farmer irrigating a crop in the dry period between the monsoons
A Malabar farmer who sows a crop with the southwest monsoon rain in June
A Coromandel farmer who sows a crop with the northeast monsoon rain in October
A farmer who plans no sowing between the two monsoon periods and keeps the field idle

questions.q: A student writes, 'North Indian farmers have no water in the dry period, so they cannot grow any crop then.' Which sentence from the chapter's account contradicts her?
questions.a: The chapter says that, in the dry period between the monsoons, farmers in north India rely on groundwater, water from rivers, canals and ponds, and moisture retained in the soil to irrigate their crops. The other statements are true but do not speak about north India's dry-period water.
o: North Indian farmers use groundwater, rivers, canals, ponds and soil moisture
The northeast monsoon prevails from October to December and rains on the east and south
The southwest monsoon brings rain from June to September, crucial for kharif crops
Coastal regions such as Malabar and Coromandel get rain from both monsoons

questions.q: A planner claims: 'Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh grow rice in every season, so irrigation is unnecessary there.' Which statement from the chapter contradicts the planner's conclusion that irrigation is unnecessary there?
questions.a: The chapter explains the all-year rice by the availability of water from the monsoon as well as from irrigation, so irrigation is part of the explanation. The other statements are true or agree with the planner's first sentence, but do not mention irrigation.
o: They grow rice all year on account of monsoon water as well as irrigation
They are among the states where rice is grown throughout the year without a break
They receive water from the monsoon, which waters their rice in the rainy months
They are named as examples from the south and the east of India

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon.
Reason (R): The terms kharif, rabi and zaid are of Arabic origin and have been used since Mughal times.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the Arabic origin of the word says nothing about why kharif crops are sown with the monsoon, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: If the monsoon is a month late, the crops the chapter names as dependent on its timely arrival are the kharif crops, while winter crops such as wheat, sown in cool weather, are not the ones the chapter singles out for this risk.
questions.a: True. The chapter says kharif crops are dependent on the timely arrival of the monsoons; rabi crops are the winter crops sown in cool weather, and the chapter names no such dependence for them.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: kharif crops depend on the timely monsoon, whereas rabi crops are winter crops sown in cool weather

questions.q:
Match each farmer's situation in Column A with the word in Column B that the chapter links to it.
Column A: 1. Sowing wheat in winter, in cool weather  2. Sowing rice with the monsoon  3. Growing watermelon in the summer  4. The period from which the Arabic season names have been in use
Column B: a. Kedara  b. Haimana  c. Graishmika  d. Mughal times
questions.a: Wheat is a rabi (winter) crop, whose older name is haimana; rice is a kharif (monsoon) crop, the older name for which is kedara (wet crops); watermelon is a zaid (summer) crop, older name graishmika. The Arabic terms have been in use since Mughal times. The wrong options swap the three older names.

questions.q: Baban has bajra seed and wheat seed. The monsoon is a month late. Which statement is right, going by the chapter?
questions.a: Bajra is a kharif crop and the chapter says kharif crops depend on the timely arrival of the monsoons. Wheat is a rabi crop sown in cool weather. The wrong options swap the seasons, extend the risk to all crops or misplace bajra in the summer season.
o: Only the bajra plan is at risk, as kharif crops depend on a timely monsoon
Only the wheat plan is at risk, because rabi crops are the monsoon crops of the year
Both plans are at risk equally, because every crop depends on the monsoon's arrival
Neither plan is at risk, because bajra is a zaid crop and wheat a rabi crop

questions.q: Neha says, 'The three cropping seasons follow the weather: kharif is the monsoon, rabi is the winter and zaid is the summer.' Is she right? Support your answer with one crop for each season from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter calls kharif the monsoon crops (for example rice or maize), rabi the winter crops sown in cool weather (for example wheat or mustard) and zaid the summer crops (for example watermelon or cucumber).
s: Verdict: agrees
Matches each season with its weather: monsoon, winter, summer
One correct crop for each of the three seasons

questions.q: A farmer's seed list reads: wheat, barley, mustard, cotton. (a) Which crop is the odd one out? (b) What do the other three share, in season and weather?
questions.a: (a) Cotton, a kharif crop. (b) Wheat, barley and mustard are rabi crops, the winter crops sown in cool weather.
s: (a) cotton, a kharif crop
(b) the other three are rabi crops, winter crops sown in cool weather

questions.q:
A village has 10 hectares: bajra 4, groundnut 2, wheat 3 and cucumber 1. This year the monsoon is a month late. The panchayat has a fund of ₹12,000 to help with the cost of re-sowing. Re-sowing costs ₹3,000 per hectare for bajra and ₹6,000 per hectare for groundnut.
(a) Which of the village's crops does the chapter say depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon, and what area is under them?
(b) What fraction of the village's land is that?
(c) What does it cost to re-sow all the bajra, and all the groundnut? Can the fund cover both?
(d) The fund can cover only one crop. Which would you support, and why?
questions.a: (a) Bajra and groundnut, both kharif crops: 4 + 2 = 6 hectares. (b) 6 / 10 = 3/5 (60 per cent). (c) Bajra: 4 x 3,000 = ₹12,000; groundnut: 2 x 6,000 = ₹12,000; each uses the whole fund, so it cannot cover both. (d) A reasoned choice: bajra covers twice the area (4 ha against 2 ha) for the same money; groundnut is a smaller area that costs twice as much per hectare. Either can be defended with the figures.
s: Part (a): bajra and groundnut as kharif crops, 6 hectares
Part (b): 3/5 or 60 per cent
Part (c): ₹12,000 for each crop, so the fund cannot cover both
Part (d): a choice supported by the area and the cost per hectare

questions.q: A 40-hectare farm uses three-fifths of its land for kharif crops and one-tenth for zaid crops. If every hectare belongs to exactly one of the chapter's three cropping seasons, the area under rabi crops is ___ hectares.

Read the statements.
1. Rabi crops such as wheat, barley, peas, mustard and gram are winter crops sown in cool weather.
2. Zaid crops are grown in the monsoon, so they include rice and maize.
3. Kharif crops can never be harmed by heavy rainfall, because they are monsoon crops.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 1 is correct. 2 is false because zaid crops are summer crops such as watermelon and cucumber. 3 is false: the chapter says excessive rainfall destroys crops.
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Village X grows only rice, cotton and groundnut. Village Y grows rice, wheat, mustard, cucumber and muskmelon. In a year the monsoon arrives a month late. Evaluate which village's food supply is more exposed, using the chapter's ideas on the three cropping seasons.
questions.a: Village X grows only kharif crops (rice, cotton, groundnut), and the chapter says kharif crops depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon, so a late monsoon puts all its crops at risk. Village Y grows kharif rice too, but also rabi crops (wheat, mustard) and zaid crops (cucumber, muskmelon), which the chapter does not single out for this risk. The rhythm of the three seasons makes a wide variety of products available through the year and helps ensure food supply. So X is more exposed; Y is not free of risk because its rice is a kharif crop.
s: Classifies X's crops as kharif and Y's as kharif, rabi and zaid
Kharif crops depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon
Y has rabi and zaid crops that the chapter does not name as dependent on it
The rhythm of the seasons ensures variety and food supply through the year
Verdict: X is more exposed, but Y's rice is also at risk

questions.q: A garden has jowar, wheat and cucumber. Ritu says it uses all three cropping seasons. Imran says it uses only two, because jowar and cucumber both grow in hot weather. Who is right, going by the chapter?
questions.a: Jowar is listed with the kharif (monsoon) crops, wheat with the rabi (winter) crops and cucumber with the zaid (summer) crops, so all three seasons are used. The wrong options misplace jowar in another season.
o: Ritu: jowar is kharif, wheat rabi and cucumber zaid, so all three seasons are used
Imran: jowar and cucumber are both zaid crops, so only two seasons are used in the garden
Imran: jowar and wheat are both rabi crops, so only two seasons are used in the garden
Ritu: but only because jowar is a rabi crop and wheat a zaid crop, with cucumber kharif

questions.q: A family's meals include rice in the monsoon months, wheat rotis in winter and watermelon in summer. Using the chapter, (a) name the cropping season of each food, (b) say what the chapter says the rhythm of seasons ensures, and (c) say what would happen to the variety on the table if all farmers grew only kharif crops.
questions.a: (a) Rice: kharif; wheat: rabi; watermelon: zaid. (b) The rhythm makes a wide variety of agricultural products available throughout the year and ensures food supply. (c) Only kharif products would be available, so the wheat and the watermelon (the rabi and zaid products) would be missing.
s: (a) kharif, rabi, zaid for rice, wheat, watermelon
(b) variety available through the year and a food supply
(c) the rabi and zaid foods would be missing if only kharif crops were grown

questions.q: The Arthashastra says a good rainy season is one when one-third of the annual rainfall comes at the beginning (Shravana, July-August) and at the end (Kartika, October-November) of the season, and two-thirds in the middle (August-September and September-October). (a) On a 1,200 mm year, how much rain should fall in the middle months on this pattern? (b) The book hints that this statement may have to do with the crop cycle. Name one cropping season it could serve and give a reason from the quoted rain pattern.
questions.a: (a) Two-thirds of 1,200 mm = 800 mm. (b) A reasoned link to either season is accepted. For example, kharif: the early rain in July-August suits sowing and the heavy middle months suit growing monsoon crops; or rabi: the late rain in October-November leaves moisture for winter crops.
s: (b) a season named (kharif or rabi) with a reason linked to the rain periods in the quotation

questions.q: The caption of the chapter's chart of kharif, rabi and zaid crops says it shows the crops and seasons 'in most parts of India'. A student says the chart fits every district exactly. What does the caption show about her claim?
questions.a: The caption says the pattern holds in most parts of India, not in all of them, so a claim that it fits every district exactly goes beyond what the chart says. The wrong options invent facts the caption does not state.
o: It goes too far, because the caption says only 'most parts' of India
It is right, because the chart lists every crop grown in every district of India
It is right, because the three seasons are fixed by law for every district in India
It goes too far, because the chart gives only the rabi season and nothing on the others

questions.q: Anita has only wheat and mustard seed in her store. (a) In which cropping season, and in what kind of weather, should she sow them? (b) A neighbour tells her to sow them with the first monsoon rain. Which season would that put them in, and why does it not match the chapter's grouping?
questions.a: (a) The rabi season, in winter, in cool weather. (b) The monsoon is the kharif season; the chapter groups wheat and mustard with rabi, the winter crops sown in cool weather, not with the monsoon crops.
s: (a) rabi, winter, cool weather
(b) the monsoon is kharif; wheat and mustard are rabi crops

questions.q:
A village in Madhya Pradesh grows these crops on 200 hectares. Rice 40, wheat 55, gram 25, groundnut 20, watermelon 6, cucumber 4, cotton 30, mustard 20 (hectares).
(a) Sort the crops into kharif, rabi and zaid and find the area under each season.
(b) Which season's crops are most at risk if the monsoon arrives late, and why?
(c) What fraction of the village's 200 hectares is under those crops?
(d) The panchayat can fund water support for only one group: the kharif fields or the 10 hectares of zaid crops. Which would you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Kharif: rice, groundnut, cotton = 90 ha. Rabi: wheat, gram, mustard = 100 ha. Zaid: watermelon, cucumber = 10 ha. (b) Kharif crops, because they depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon. (c) 90 / 200 = 9/20 (45 per cent). (d) A choice with a reason: the kharif fields are nine times the zaid area and rely on a monsoon that is late; the zaid crops grow in summer and need water whatever the monsoon does.
s: Part (a): 90, 100 and 10 hectares correctly sorted
Part (b): kharif, because of reliance on the timely monsoon
Part (c): 9/20 or 45 per cent
Part (d): a choice that uses the hectares and the monsoon dependence

questions.q: A history teacher says, 'The Mughals introduced the whole system of farming in three seasons.' Which comment fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says farmers have followed the rhythm for centuries, and that the Arabic terms have been in use since Mughal times; before that the crops were called kedara, haimana and graishmika. The wrong options date the rhythm itself to the Mughals.
o: Farmers followed the rhythm for centuries; only the Arabic names date from Mughal times
The three seasons began in Mughal times, along with the Arabic names for them
Arab traders first described the three seasons and gave India its main crops
Farmers had no names for the seasons before the Mughals, so no seasonal rhythm existed before then

questions.q: A panchayat says, 'A town whose farmers grow only wheat has the same food security as one whose farmers follow the kharif, rabi and zaid rhythm.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is not supported. Wheat is a rabi crop, so a wheat-only town depends on one season's harvest and one kind of food. The chapter says the rhythm of kharif (for example rice and maize), rabi (for example wheat and mustard) and zaid (for example watermelon and cucumber) makes a wide variety of products available throughout the year and is one of the factors that ensure food supply. A town following the rhythm has harvests in each season, though its kharif crops carry the risk of a late monsoon or excessive rain.
s: Wheat is a rabi crop, so the town depends on one season
The rhythm of three seasons makes a variety of products available through the year
One example crop each from the other two seasons
The rhythm is one of the factors that ensures food supply
A verdict that the claim is not supported

questions.q: Write a four-line riddle whose answer is 'rabi'. Use at least three facts from the chapter, such as the weather, the season and the crops.
questions.a: Any riddle using three correct facts, e.g. I am sown when the weather is cool; wheat, gram and mustard are mine; I am the winter crop season; my name came into use in Mughal times and haimana was my older name.
s: First correct fact in the riddle
Second correct fact
Third correct fact and a clear single answer 'rabi'

questions.q: Four statements about the cropping seasons are given. Which one is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter links kharif crops to the timely monsoon, notes that excessive rainfall destroys crops and says the rhythm helps ensure food supply. It describes zaid crops as summer crops and says nothing about the northeast monsoon watering them.
o: Zaid crops depend on the northeast monsoon from October to December
Kharif crops depend on the timely arrival of the monsoons each year
Excessive rainfall also leads to the destruction of crops and distress
The rhythm of the three seasons helps ensure the food supply for the people

questions.q: A village grows rice on 24 hectares, gram on 18, mustard on 12 and cucumber on 6. (a) Find the area under each of the three cropping seasons. (b) How many times the zaid area is the rabi area?
questions.a: (a) Kharif (rice): 24 ha; rabi (gram, mustard): 18 + 12 = 30 ha; zaid (cucumber): 6 ha. (b) 30 / 6 = 5 times.
s: (a) 24, 30 and 6 hectares correctly sorted
(b) 5 times

questions.q: Meera says, 'Red soil and laterite soil are the same, because both are reddish from iron.' (a) Name one thing the chapter says they share. (b) Give one difference in how they form or behave that shows they are not the same.
questions.a: (a) Both owe a reddish colour to iron reacting with air and water, and neither is fertile (red is 'not very fertile', laterite 'not fertile'). (b) Red soil forms by weathering of lava that cooled slowly or of old rocks; laterite forms by weathering of rock by rain, which washes most minerals away, and it becomes hard in hot weather.
s: (a) reddish colour from iron, or low fertility
(b) a difference: red from lava or old rocks; laterite from rain weathering, losing minerals, hardening in heat

questions.q: A block of 600 hectares has 40 per cent alluvial soil, 25 per cent black soil and the rest red soil. The area under the two soils the chapter calls rich in nutrients or very fertile is ___ hectares.

Write a short situation (three or four lines) in which a farmer improves a worn-out plot of red or laterite soil using what the chapter says humus does. Name the soil, say why it needs help, and say what the added humus gives it.
questions.a: Any valid situation, e.g. Sita's plot of laterite soil is not fertile because rain has washed away most of its minerals. She spreads rotted leaves and dung that decompose into humus, which is rich in nutrients and retains moisture, so the plot can feed her crop and hold water longer.
s: Names red or laterite soil and says why it needs help (not fertile or not very fertile)
Adds decaying plant or animal matter that forms humus
States what humus gives: nutrients and moisture retention

questions.q: A farmer owns four plots, one each of alluvial, black, red and laterite soil, and can afford extra compost for only one plot this year. Compare the fertility of the four soils as the chapter describes it, say which plot you would give the compost to, and justify your choice using what humus does.
questions.a: The chapter calls alluvial soil rich in nutrients, black soil very fertile, red soil not very fertile and laterite soil not fertile. Humus is dark organic matter, rich in nutrients and able to retain moisture. A reasoned choice: the laterite plot, as the least fertile, gains most from added nutrients and moisture retention (its minerals have been washed away); or the red plot, which is already somewhat fertile, may respond best. The alluvial and black plots are already rich and need the compost least.
s: Fertility of all four soils correctly stated
A plot chosen (laterite or red)
Reason using humus: nutrients and moisture retention
Explains why alluvial and black plots are lower priority

questions.q:
The Eco Club of a school in Wardha digs a soil pit at the edge of a farm and records the layers from the bottom. Layer 1: solid rock. Layer 2: rock that is breaking into pieces. Layer 3: dark topsoil full of decayed leaves and roots, in which beans are growing. The farm owner, Mr Gaikwad, earns about ₹20,000 a year from beans on this half acre. A brick-maker offers ₹50,000 once for the top 30 cm of soil from it.
(a) What is the dark organic matter in Layer 3 called, and how is it formed?
(b) What name does the chapter give to the rock of Layer 1, and what process breaks it into soil particles?
(c) How long does the chapter say soil formation takes, and why does that matter to Mr Gaikwad?
(d) The offer equals how many years of his bean income? Should he accept it? Decide and justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Humus, formed by the decomposition of plant and animal matter. (b) Bedrock; weathering. (c) The chapter's text says soil forms over millions of years, and its figure says the process ranges from a century to several millennia; either way soil removed cannot be replaced within his lifetime. (d) ₹50,000 / ₹20,000 = 2.5 years of income. A reasoned decision: refusing is supported because the topsoil with its humus gives the crops nutrients, water and support and is slow to form, while accepting can be defended as a lump sum if a plan restores the soil.
s: Part (a): humus from decomposed plants and animals
Part (b): bedrock; weathering
Part (c): millions of years (text) or a century to several millennia (figure); it cannot be quickly replaced
Part (d): 2.5 years, and a decision that uses the nutrients and slow formation of topsoil

questions.q: True or False: Red soil and laterite soil both owe a reddish colour to iron, but only laterite is described as having most of its minerals washed away.
questions.a: True. The chapter says red soil is red because of iron and is not very fertile; for laterite it says rain washes most minerals away, leaving largely iron and aluminium, which give the reddish colour, and it is not fertile.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: both are reddish through iron, but the washing away of minerals is stated only for laterite

questions.q: A student says, 'Alluvial soil and black soil are the same, because both are fertile.' (a) Give the source of each soil. (b) Name one feature the chapter gives for black soil that its description of alluvial soil does not.
questions.a: (a) Alluvial soil: silt brought by rivers from the mountains and plateaus. Black soil: weathering of volcanic rocks. (b) Black soil holds a lot of moisture (and is called cotton soil).
s: (a) alluvial from river silt; black from weathered volcanic rock
(b) holds a lot of moisture, or the name cotton soil

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Laterite soil is not fertile.
Reason (R): Rain washes most of the minerals out of the weathered rock, leaving largely iron and aluminium.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true: the chapter says that in laterite soil most minerals get washed away, leaving largely iron and aluminium, and that the soil is not fertile. Losing the minerals that plants need is what explains the lack of fertility, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A teacher describes four things seen on a hill-and-river field trip in Column A. Match each with the chapter's term in Column B.
Column A: 1. A rock on the hillside crumbling into soil particles through rain, ice or living roots  2. Dark matter made of rotted leaves and animals that holds moisture and nutrients  3. Fine dust-like sediment that the river carries down to the plain  4. The solid original rock under the soil, from which new soils are derived
Column B: a. Silt  b. Bedrock  c. Weathering  d. Humus
questions.a: Weathering is the breaking down of rocks and minerals into soil particles; humus is dark organic matter from decomposed plant and animal matter; silt is the fine sediment rivers carry; bedrock is the original rock from which soils derive. The wrong options swap the terms for the process and the material.

questions.q: The Amarakosha described twelve types of agricultural land based on soil fertility. (a) Why is fertility, and not colour, a sounder basis for grading land, using red soil and laterite soil as evidence? (b) Which of the six major soil types today would the Amarakosha's basis put at the top?
questions.a: (a) Red soil and laterite are both reddish because of iron, yet red soil is not very fertile and laterite is not fertile, so colour tells little about fertility. (b) Alluvial soil (rich in nutrients) or black soil (very fertile).
s: (a) two soils of similar colour with low fertility, so colour does not show fertility
(b) alluvial or black soil at the top

questions.q: The Himalayas give rise to two very different soils, alluvial soil on the river plains and alpine soil on the high slopes. Explain why the two differ, using what the chapter says about how each forms, how silt is carried, and what each soil is like.
questions.a: Alpine soil is formed on the high slopes by the freezing and melting of ice, which weathers the rock; the soil stays thin, rough and rocky. Rivers, on the other hand, carry silt, a fine-grained dust-like sediment of rock and mineral particles larger than clay and smaller than sand, from the mountains and plateaus down to the plains. This silt is deposited as alluvial soil, which is rich in nutrients. So where weathered material stays on the slope it is thin and rocky, while the fine particles that rivers carry down and deposit on the plains give rich soil.
s: Alpine soil formed by freezing and melting of ice weathering rock
Alpine soil is thin, rough and rocky
Silt is fine-grained, so rivers easily carry it from the mountains
Alluvial soil formed from silt deposits on the plains, rich in nutrients
Links the two: carried-down fine material versus weathered material left on the slope

questions.q: A cotton grower has two unirrigated plots to choose from, one of black soil and one of red soil. Which choice does the chapter's description of the two soils support?
questions.a: Black soil, formed from weathered volcanic rock, holds a lot of moisture and is very fertile; it is also called cotton soil. Red soil owes its colour to iron and is not very fertile. The wrong options credit red soil with fertility or moisture.
o: The black soil plot, which holds a lot of moisture and is very fertile
The red soil plot, since its iron makes it very fertile and moisture-rich
The red soil plot, since it holds more moisture than black soil does
Either plot, as soil colour decides nothing about fertility or moisture

questions.q:
A district of 20,000 hectares has four zones. Valley floor with river silt: 5,000 ha. Lava plateau with weathered volcanic rock: 8,000 ha. Old-rock uplands where the soil is red because of iron and is not very fertile: 5,000 ha. High slopes with thin, rocky soil: 2,000 ha. The government plans to grow cotton on one zone and to bring irrigation to one other zone.
(a) Which soil type is in each zone?
(b) What per cent of the district has the fertile soils of the valley and the plateau?
(c) Which zone is best suited to cotton, and what is the soil's other name?
(d) Irrigation can be given either to the 5,000 ha of reddish soil or to the 2,000 ha of high slopes. Which will you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Valley: alluvial; plateau: black; uplands: red; slopes: alpine. (b) 13,000 / 20,000 = 65 per cent. (c) The lava plateau with black soil, also called cotton soil. (d) Any choice with a reason: red soil is not very fertile but crops can be grown on it with efficient irrigation and the area is larger; the thin, rough, rocky alpine soil would gain little and covers only 2,000 ha.
s: Part (a): alluvial, black, red, alpine
Part (b): 65 per cent
Part (c): the plateau, black or cotton soil
Part (d): a choice backed by area, fertility or the role of irrigation

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Soil is formed through the breakdown of rocks and the decay of organic matter.
2. Humus, formed by the decomposition of plant and animal matter, is rich in nutrients and retains moisture in the soil.
3. Red soil gets its colour from iron and is therefore very fertile.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 follow the chapter. 3 is false: red soil is reddish because of iron, but the chapter calls it not very fertile.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A student sieves a sample of river-plain soil into three heaps: sand, clay and silt. Using the chapter's description of silt, which order runs from the finest to the coarsest particles?
questions.a: The chapter describes silt as particles larger than clay but smaller than sand, so the order from finest to coarsest is clay, silt, sand. The wrong options put silt outside that middle place.
o: Clay, silt, sand
Silt, clay, sand
Sand, silt, clay
Clay, sand, silt

questions.q: Tarun says, 'Soil is made by both rocks and living things: rock breaks down, and plants and animals add to it.' Is he right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says soil is formed through the breakdown of rocks (weathering of the bedrock) and the decay of organic matter; the formation diagram says organic materials facilitate the disintegration of rock, and humus, formed from decomposed plant and animal matter, enriches the soil.
s: Verdict: agrees
Rocks: breakdown of rocks or bedrock by weathering
Living things: decay of organic matter forming humus, which enriches the soil

questions.q: After years of adding rotted crop residue and dung, a farmer's worn-out field is darker and stays moist longer. Her neighbour says the colour change shows the field has turned into black soil. What is the better explanation, going by the chapter?
questions.a: Humus is dark organic matter formed by decomposition of plant and animal matter; it is rich in nutrients and retains moisture. Black soil is a major soil type formed by weathering of volcanic rocks. The wrong options confuse humus with soil types.
o: Humus has built up from decayed matter; black soil is a different soil type
Black soil forms whenever dung or crop residue is added to any field for some years
Humus is another name for black soil, so the field has changed its soil type
The field has turned into alluvial soil, as dung is a kind of silt from rivers

questions.q: Ravi farms on a river plain and wants soil rich in nutrients that comes from silt brought by rivers. Uma farms on a plateau without irrigation and wants soil that holds a lot of moisture. Which pair of soils fits them, going by the chapter?
questions.a: Alluvial soil is silt deposited by rivers and is rich in nutrients; black soil, from weathered volcanic rock, holds a lot of moisture. Laterite is not fertile and hardens in hot weather.
o: Ravi: alluvial soil; Uma: black soil
Ravi: black soil; Uma: alluvial soil
Ravi: alluvial soil; Uma: laterite soil
Ravi: laterite soil; Uma: black soil

questions.q: The chapter's soil map of India carries the note that most regions will have local variations. A farmer in the black-soil area finds one patch of reddish soil on her farm. What does the note suggest?
