questions.a: The figure's caption says most regions will have local variations, so a patch that differs from the map's main soil is to be expected. The wrong options treat the map as perfectly exact or as completely wrong.
o: It is expected, since local variations occur within mapped soil areas
The map is wrong in this region and should not be used by farmers at all
Her whole farm must really be red soil, whatever the map shows
The reddish patch proves black soil cannot form in her area

questions.q: (a) Which soil does the chapter name for the Ganga basin, and how does it describe it? (b) Using the description of silt, explain why a river basin may have such a soil.
questions.a: (a) Alluvial soil, described as rich. (b) Silt is a fine-grained, dust-like sediment, so rivers easily carry it from the mountains to the plains, where it is deposited and forms alluvial soil.
s: (a) alluvial soil, rich
(b) fine silt is easily carried by rivers and deposited on the plains

questions.q: In the book's figure of crops grown in different soil areas, a note says that crops marked with an asterisk are not on the ideal soil for their cultivation but can be grown with efficient irrigation. What does this show about the link between soil and crops, and what can make up for a less ideal soil?
questions.a: Soil strongly influences which crops thrive, which is why most crops are shown on their ideal soils. Efficient irrigation can make up for a less ideal soil.
s: Soil strongly influences which crops grow well
Efficient irrigation can make up for a less ideal soil
Links the two: the starred crops are possible on less ideal soil only because of irrigation

questions.q: Savita grows several crops in the same field, choosing them so that something is harvested at regular intervals. (a) Which traditional method of the chapter is this? (b) Give two benefits the chapter mentions, and say how this method differs from crop rotation.
questions.a: (a) Multiple cropping. (b) It reduces the risk of pests and ensures at least one crop. It differs from crop rotation, which grows different crops in the same field in different seasons to stop the soil losing specific nutrients.
s: Part (a): multiple cropping
Part (b): two benefits (fewer pests, at least one crop) and the contrast with rotation

questions.q: Class 7 holds a debate on the motion 'Traditional irrigation methods are better than modern ones.' Prepare a balanced speech using the chapter. Include two traditional and two modern methods with how each works, one point for the traditional side, one for the modern side, and your own conclusion.
questions.a: Traditional: the phad system of Maharashtra is community-based and uses small canals to divert river water; bamboo drip irrigation in northeastern India uses bamboo pipes to channel spring water to fields. Modern: drip irrigation delivers water slowly to the roots through tubes and emitters; sprinkler irrigation sprays water into the air like artificial rain. For the traditional side: these systems use local sources and, as with the community-based phad, are shared by the community. For the modern side: they use water more efficiently, which matters because groundwater reserves are fast decreasing, and they allow farming in low-rainfall areas. A balanced conclusion: each suits different needs, and neither can be called better without the place and the water source in mind.
s: Two traditional methods with how they work
Two modern methods with how they work
A point for the traditional side based on the chapter
A point for the modern side: efficiency, falling groundwater or farming in low-rainfall areas
A reasoned conclusion

questions.q: On her hill farm, Ritu spreads cow dung to restore nutrients and ploughs along the natural curves of the slope. Her son plants trees along the hill and cuts flat steps into it. Which grouping of these four practices matches the chapter's headings of traditional methods and contemporary approaches?
questions.a: The chapter lists organic fertilisers such as cow dung and contour ploughing among the traditional methods, and terracing and afforestation (planting trees) among the contemporary approaches. The wrong options mix the two groups.
o: Traditional: cow dung and contour ploughing; contemporary: planting trees and terracing
Traditional: planting trees and terracing; contemporary: cow dung and contour ploughing
Traditional: cow dung and terracing; contemporary: planting trees and contour ploughing
Traditional: contour ploughing and planting trees; contemporary: cow dung and terracing

questions.q: Rani's village gets sufficient monsoon rain and she uses no canal or pump. A neighbour says, 'Since your area gets enough rain, nothing can go wrong for your farm.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says rain-fed agriculture relies entirely on rainfall and is common in areas that receive sufficient rain in the monsoon, yet rain-fed farmers face droughts and unpredictable monsoons. Irrigated agriculture uses artificial methods to supply water.
o: Her farming is rain-fed, yet she can face droughts and unpredictable monsoons
Her farming is irrigated, because monsoon rain is a natural form of irrigation
Her farming is rain-fed, so droughts and unpredictable monsoons cannot touch it
Her farming is irrigated, since sufficient rain removes all challenges

questions.q: A farmer buys a drip set that costs ₹60,000 per hectare and has a grant of ₹2,10,000. The number of hectares she can cover is ___.
True or False: Soil conservation, as the chapter defines it, means only adding fertiliser to a field.
questions.a: False. The chapter defines soil conservation as managing soil to prevent its degradation and preserve its productivity; the methods include crop rotation, contour ploughing, terracing, afforestation and mulching as well as fertilisers.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: conservation prevents degradation and preserves productivity, using many methods besides fertiliser

questions.q: Ishita says, 'Panchagavya is only an old belief and has no proven benefit.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. Panchagavya is a fermented mixture of dung, urine, milk, curd and ghee, and recent studies have shown that it acts as a biofertiliser, enhancing crop growth and productivity and increasing resistance to disease.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Names what panchagavya is
Recent studies show biofertiliser effect and higher productivity or disease resistance

questions.q: A farmer says, 'Soil conservation is a waste of effort: soil is only dead earth.' Evaluate this using the chapter. Explain what the chapter says soil contains, what the living part does, what soil conservation means, and give two conservation methods with the problem each prevents.
questions.a: The claim is not supported. The chapter calls soil a complex ecosystem with bacteria, fungi, earthworms and insects, together with minerals, organic matter (humus), water and air. The organisms break down organic material and improve the health of the soil so that it can sustain healthy plants. Soil conservation is managing soil to prevent its degradation and preserve its productivity. For example, crop rotation (different crops in different seasons) stops the soil losing specific nutrients, and contour ploughing along the curves of a slope avoids erosion by rainwater.
s: Soil is an ecosystem with living organisms and also minerals, humus, water and air
The organisms break down organic material and improve soil health for plants
Soil conservation: managing soil to prevent degradation and preserve productivity
Two methods, each with the problem it prevents
A verdict that the claim is not supported

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Rain-fed farming relies entirely on rainfall, so droughts and unpredictable monsoons are no problem for it.
2. Contour ploughing means ploughing along the natural curves of a hill slope to avoid soil erosion from rainwater.
3. Sprinkler irrigation delivers water slowly and directly to the roots through tubes and emitters.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 2 is correct. 1 is false: farmers who depend on rain face droughts and unpredictable monsoons. 3 describes drip irrigation, while sprinklers spray water like artificial rain.
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: A district official writes in a report, 'Bamboo drip irrigation is just another name for the modern drip irrigation.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter lists bamboo drip irrigation among traditional systems, where farmers use bamboo pipes to channel water from springs to fields in parts of northeastern India. Modern drip irrigation delivers water slowly to the roots through tubes and emitters. Sprinklers spray water.
o: They differ: bamboo drip uses bamboo pipes and spring water; modern drip uses tubes and emitters
They differ: bamboo drip uses tubes and emitters, while modern drip uses bamboo pipes and spring water
They are the same, since both are traditional systems of Maharashtra using canals
They differ: bamboo drip sprays water into the air, while modern drip delivers it to the roots

questions.q: Mohan says, 'With irrigation, farmers no longer need to bother about the monsoon or about how much water they use.' Is he right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Only partly. Irrigation helps: it reduces reliance on monsoon rains, enables farming even in areas of low rainfall and gives a more stable food supply. But groundwater reserves are fast decreasing in many parts of India, so water has to be used efficiently, which is why modern methods such as drip and sprinkler irrigation are needed.
s: Verdict: partly right
Irrigation reduces reliance on the monsoon and allows farming in low-rainfall areas
Groundwater is fast decreasing, so efficient use is necessary

questions.q:
Chandrakala farms 3 hectares in a low-rainfall village of Marathwada. She has no canal or well, only a small pond that collects rainwater. For the dry months she can fit either a drip set at ₹60,000 per hectare or a sprinkler set at ₹25,000 per hectare. She has ₹1,20,000 to spend.
(a) Is her farming rain-fed or irrigated, and what does the chapter say a small pond does for the soil?
(b) How does drip irrigation deliver water, and how do sprinklers differ?
(c) How many hectares can she cover with ₹1,20,000 under each choice, up to her 3 hectares?
(d) Which would you advise her to buy, and why?
questions.a: (a) Rain-fed; a small pond collects rainwater and provides moisture to the soil for a longer period. (b) Drip delivers water slowly and directly to the roots through tubes and emitters; sprinklers spray water into the air, to fall like artificial rain. (c) Drip: 1,20,000 / 60,000 = 2 hectares. Sprinkler: all 3 hectares, costing ₹75,000. (d) A defended choice: drip uses water most efficiently at the roots but covers only 2 of her 3 hectares; sprinklers cover all 3 hectares and leave ₹45,000, but water is sprayed over the whole crop.
s: Part (a): rain-fed; the pond keeps moisture in the soil longer
Part (b): drip at the roots; sprinklers like rain
Part (c): 2 hectares and 3 hectares
Part (d): a choice that weighs area covered against water efficiency

questions.q: Sort these five practices into those that mainly protect the soil from erosion and those that mainly protect its nutrients: terracing, crop rotation, contour ploughing, cow dung as fertiliser, afforestation. (a) Name the erosion group. (b) Name the nutrient group and the effect of one of its practices.
questions.a: (a) Erosion: terracing, contour ploughing, afforestation. (b) Nutrients: crop rotation (different crops in different seasons so the soil does not lose specific nutrients) and cow dung (an organic fertiliser that replenishes the soil's nutrients).
s: (a) terracing, contour ploughing and afforestation
(b) crop rotation and cow dung, with the effect of one

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In many parts of India, groundwater reserves are fast decreasing.
Reason (R): Drip and sprinkler irrigation help to use water more efficiently.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but efficient irrigation is a response to falling groundwater, not the cause of it, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Write a short situation (three or four lines) in which a farmer would prefer irrigated farming to rain-fed farming. Then name one traditional structure or system and one modern method she could use.
questions.a: Any valid situation, e.g. a farmer in a dry area with an unpredictable monsoon. Traditional: any of kull, kund, ahar, pokhar, khadin, arakere, eri, phad, bamboo drip, farm ponds or Kallanai-type structures. Modern: drip or sprinkler irrigation.
s: Situation that justifies irrigation
One traditional system named
One modern method named

questions.q: A farmer applies fertiliser only in the exact amounts her crop needs. Which two gains does the chapter name for such very precise application?
questions.a: The chapter says very precise application of fertilisers enables their efficient use and also maintains soil health. Flat steps are terracing; a windbreak and another crop come from banana trees on bunds; the last option is the opposite of the chapter.
o: Efficient use of the fertiliser and the maintenance of soil health
Flat steps that slow runoff and a cheaper harvest every year
A windbreak for the field and another crop to sell from the bunds
More nutrients lost from the soil and faster erosion of the topsoil

questions.q:
Match each farm problem in Column A with the measure in Column B that the chapter links to it.
Column A: 1. Rainwater runs down a hillside and washes the soil away  2. The same crop keeps taking the same nutrients from a field  3. Groundwater is fast decreasing and water must be used efficiently  4. A farmer wants windbreakers and another crop on the bunds of his paddy fields
Column B: a. Crop rotation  b. Terracing  c. Drip and sprinkler irrigation  d. Banana trees on the bunds
questions.a: Terracing slows water runoff and reduces soil erosion; crop rotation stops the soil losing specific nutrients; drip and sprinkler irrigation use water efficiently; banana trees on the bunds act as windbreakers, hold the soil and give another crop. The wrong options swap the problems.

questions.q: (a) Who built Kallanai, across which river, and in about which century CE was it built if it is about 1,800 years old and the present year is 2026? (b) Munsar Lake was built in the 11th century CE. Which is older, and by roughly how many years?
questions.a: (a) Karikala built it across the Kaveri; 2026 - 1,800 = 226, so around the 3rd century CE. (b) Kallanai is older, by roughly 775 to 875 years (any answer from about 750 to 900 years is accepted).
s: (a) Karikala, the Kaveri, about the 3rd century CE
(b) Kallanai is older, by about 750 to 900 years

questions.q:
Devraj has 5 hectares on a hill in Uttarakhand. The soil lost each year, in tonnes per hectare, is 24 when he ploughs up and down the slope, 12 when he ploughs along the natural curves of the slope, and 4 when he cuts flat steps into the hillside. Ploughing along the curves costs nothing extra. Cutting steps costs ₹80,000 per hectare, and he can spend ₹2 lakh.
(a) Name the method that ploughs along the curves and the method that cuts steps, and say what the second does to water runoff.
(b) By what per cent does ploughing along the curves cut soil loss compared with ploughing up and down?
(c) How much soil is lost a year if all 5 hectares are ploughed along the curves, and if 2.5 hectares get steps and 2.5 are ploughed along the curves?
(d) Is cutting the steps worth ₹2 lakh? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Contour ploughing; terracing creates flat steps that slow down water runoff and reduce soil erosion. (b) (24 - 12) / 24 = 50 per cent. (c) All contour: 5 x 12 = 60 tonnes. Mixed: 2.5 x 4 + 2.5 x 12 = 40 tonnes. (d) Whichever is chosen needs a reason: spending ₹2 lakh cuts annual loss by 20 more tonnes (60 to 40) and protects soil that takes millions of years to form; or the free contour method already halves the loss, so the money could go elsewhere.
s: Part (a): contour ploughing; terracing makes flat steps that slow runoff
Part (b): 50 per cent
Part (c): 60 tonnes and 40 tonnes
Part (d): a decision using the extra 20 tonnes saved and the cost

questions.q: A guide says, 'Munsar Lake at Viramgam is a natural lake that people simply began to worship.' Which detail given with the photograph in the chapter contradicts the guide?
questions.a: The chapter says the Munsar Lake is, like many lakes in Indian cities, an artificial one, constructed by Minaldevi in the 11th century CE. The shrines and temples show that water bodies have been regarded as sacred; they do not contradict the guide's description of origin.
o: It is an artificial lake built by a queen in the 11th century CE
Its banks are dotted with small shrines and a few bigger temples
It lies at Viramgam in Gujarat and was photographed from its banks
Water bodies in India have long been regarded as sacred by many people

questions.q: Village P's farmers rely on rainfall alone, while Village Q's farmers supply water to their fields by artificial methods. The monsoon turns unpredictable this year. (a) Which village's farmers face the greater risk, and why? (b) Name two adaptations the chapter says rain-fed farmers have developed.
questions.a: (a) Village P, whose rain-fed agriculture relies entirely on rainfall, so droughts and unpredictable monsoons hit it directly. (b) Choosing drought-resistant crops and using traditional water-harvesting techniques.
s: (a) Village P, because it is rain-fed
(b) drought-resistant crops and traditional water-harvesting techniques

questions.q: Before the seed drill, a farmer did soil preparation, seed planting and closing the furrow as three separate steps on each of 5 plots. Using a seed drill, each plot needs one operation, so the number of separate steps saved in all is ___.

Fig. 1.20 of the chapter shows three agricultural systems that the FAO has recognised in India: (1) a field of crocus flowers that yields saffron in Kashmir, (2) an integrated forest and land-based agricultural system in Odisha, (3) integrated paddy farming in saline water with fishing and livestock rearing in Kerala. (a) Which two of the three combine farming with another activity, and with what? (b) What do these two have in common?
questions.a: (a) The Odisha system combines farming with forest management; the Kerala system combines paddy with fishing and livestock rearing. (b) Both are integrated systems that join crop growing with other activities of the land and water, rather than a single crop on its own.
s: (a) Odisha with forest management and Kerala with fishing and livestock
(b) both integrate crops with other activities

questions.q:
A farmer compares two plots of one hectare, with grain priced at ₹20,000 per tonne. The chemical plot gives 5.0 tonnes in year 1 and 4.4 tonnes in year 5, with inputs costing ₹30,000 a year. The organic plot (compost and neem-based sprays) gives 3.8 tonnes in year 1 and 4.3 tonnes in year 5, with inputs costing ₹12,000 a year. The farmer has a loan to repay this year.
(a) Which plot follows the Green Revolution method, and name two of its inputs.
(b) Find the net income of each plot in year 1.
(c) Find the net income of each plot in year 5.
(d) Which plot should the farmer prefer? Decide and justify with the numbers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The chemical plot; high-yielding seed, fertilisers or pesticides. (b) Chemical: 5.0 x 20,000 - 30,000 = ₹70,000. Organic: 3.8 x 20,000 - 12,000 = ₹64,000. (c) Chemical: 4.4 x 20,000 - 30,000 = ₹58,000. Organic: 4.3 x 20,000 - 12,000 = ₹74,000. (d) A choice with reasons: chemical gives ₹6,000 more in year 1 for the loan, but yields fall as the soil is impoverished, and organic pulls ahead by year 5.
s: Part (a): chemical plot, two Green Revolution inputs
Part (d): decision balancing the loan against long-term soil health

questions.q: Harpreet's saved seed from a company's high-yielding crop sprouted poorly the next year, so he must buy again. Which step would best reduce his dependence on the seed companies, going by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says seeds have been passed down in families, preserved at the community level and shared, and that dependence on seed companies has drawn criticism because the seeds produced are often unsuitable for the next season.
o: Saving and sharing seeds within family and community, as farmers traditionally did
Buying the same company seed every year from the same company, as before
Giving up seeds and planting only after buying a ready-grown plant each time
Using more chemical fertiliser so that the saved seed does well next season

questions.q:
Match each farming need in Column A with the answer in Column B that the chapter gives.
Column A: 1. Protect seeds from being spoilt and shorten germination time  2. Replace a chemical pesticide with a natural one that is much less harmful to the environment  3. Fertilise without chemicals, using compost, seed cake and animal manure  4. Do soil preparation, sowing and closing of the furrow in one operation
Column B: a. Seed drill  b. Organic farming  c. Beejamrit  d. Neem-based pesticide
questions.a: Beejamrit coats seeds; neem-based pesticides are natural and less harmful; organic farming uses natural fertilisers such as compost, seed cake and manure; the ancient Indian seed drill combined the three steps in one operation. The wrong options swap the pairs.

questions.q: True or False: Because high-yielding seeds bought from a company give higher yields, a farmer can save seed from her harvest and sow it again next season with the same results.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the seeds that plants from company-developed seeds later produce are often not suitable for planting in the next season, which is why farmers become dependent on seed companies.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: seeds from such plants are often unsuitable for the next season, creating dependence on the companies

questions.q: A farmer presses oilseeds for oil and is left with the residue. (a) What does the chapter call that residue? (b) What use does the chapter name for it in sustainable agriculture?
questions.a: (a) Seed cake, the residue after oil has been extracted from seeds. (b) It is a natural fertiliser, used in organic farming in place of chemical fertilisers.
s: (a) seed cake
(b) a natural fertiliser in organic farming

questions.q: Dev says, 'The Green Revolution was a complete success, so nobody questions that kind of farming now.' Is he fully right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Only partly. It increased food grain production, especially of wheat and rice, and India became self-sufficient in food. But its limits have become visible: long-term impoverishment of soil, depletion of groundwater, contamination by pesticides and fertilisers and damage to health, so more and more agricultural scientists question its sustainability.
s: Verdict: partly right, not completely
Credits the gains: more wheat and rice, self-sufficiency in food
Gives the limits and notes that scientists question its sustainability

questions.q:
Women of Rampur village carry seeds as part of the gifts to their marital homes, and families share seeds in the community. A company offers every farmer high-yielding wheat seed that gives 36 quintals per hectare and costs ₹6,000 per hectare each year. Saved seed gives 30 quintals per hectare and costs ₹1,500 per hectare. Wheat sells at ₹2,200 per quintal.
(a) How, according to the chapter, have seeds traditionally been kept and passed on?
(b) Name one gain and the main criticism of buying company seeds.
(c) Find the income per hectare after seed costs for each kind of seed, and the difference on 3 hectares.
(d) The panchayat must choose between a village seed-sharing scheme and a contract with the company. Which would you back, and why?
questions.a: (a) Passed down in families from generation to generation, preserved at the community level and shared (in some areas women carry them as part of the gifts to their marital homes). (b) Gain: higher yield and pest resistance. Criticism: the seeds the plant later produces are often not suitable for planting in the next season, so farmers depend on the seed companies. (c) Saved seed: 30 x 2,200 - 1,500 = ₹64,500. Company seed: 36 x 2,200 - 6,000 = ₹73,200. Difference 8,700 x 3 = ₹26,100 on 3 hectares. (d) A reasoned choice: company seed pays ₹8,700 more per hectare but creates a yearly dependence and cost; a seed-sharing scheme keeps the traditional practice and independence at a lower income.
s: Part (a): passed down in families, preserved and shared in the community
Part (b): higher yield or pest resistance as a gain; dependence on companies as the criticism
Part (c): ₹64,500 and ₹73,200, difference ₹26,100 on 3 hectares
Part (d): a choice weighing the extra income against dependence

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Terrace farming helps prevent soil erosion and conserve water on hilly slopes.
Reason (R): Terrace farming is a method practised on flat plains.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: the chapter says cutting terraces into a hillside creates flat land and helps prevent soil erosion and conserve water. R is false: terrace farming is a method used on hilly slopes.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A family in Goa has cows that give manure for the fields and bullocks that plough them, and it also grows food crops, spices and medicinal plants around its home in a structured, irrigated design. Which of the chapter's examples of traditional systems does this family follow?
questions.a: Cows giving manure and bullocks ploughing is gokrishi; a varied homestead farm around the house in a structured irrigated design is kulagar, which the chapter places in the Konkan plains of Goa. Terrace farming concerns steps cut into hillsides.
o: Both gokrishi and kulagar
Gokrishi only
Kulagar only
Terrace farming and gokrishi

questions.q: (a) Name one advantage of company-developed seeds that the chapter mentions. (b) A village proposes a community seed bank in which families keep and share their seeds. Which of the chapter's two seed practices does this follow, and which concern about company seeds does it reduce?
questions.a: (a) Higher yields, or pest resistance. (b) It follows the traditional practice of preserving seeds at the community level and sharing them; it reduces dependence on seed companies.
s: (a) higher yield or pest resistance
(b) community preservation and sharing; reduces dependence on companies

questions.q: After a village adopts Green Revolution methods, the following are observed: (i) wheat and rice output rises sharply; (ii) the water level in wells falls year after year; (iii) bees visit the flowers less. Link each observation to what the chapter says about the Green Revolution.
questions.a: (i) A gain: the revolution led to a significant increase in food grain production, particularly of wheat and rice. (ii) A limit: depletion of groundwater. (iii) A limit: the use of chemicals disrupts the ecosystem by harming important creatures like bees, which are necessary for pollination.
s: (i) matched to the increase in wheat and rice production
(ii) matched to depletion of groundwater
(iii) matched to harm to bees and pollination from chemicals

questions.q: After using high-yielding seed, irrigation and fertiliser, a farmer's wheat rises from 2.0 to 3.5 tonnes per hectare, and his yearly costs rise from ₹8,000 to ₹26,000. Grain sells at ₹20,000 per tonne. (a) Find his net income per hectare before and after. (b) Name one long-term limit of this approach, according to the chapter, that he should watch.
questions.a: (a) Before: 2.0 x 20,000 - 8,000 = ₹32,000. After: 3.5 x 20,000 - 26,000 = ₹44,000. (b) Any one of: long-term impoverishment of the soil, depletion of groundwater, contamination of soil and water by fertilisers and pesticides, damage to health.
s: (a) ₹32,000 before and ₹44,000 after
(b) one limit named from the chapter

questions.q: In one village, yields keep falling and the water table keeps dropping, even though farmers use more fertiliser and pump more groundwater each year. Which explanation fits the chapter's view of the Green Revolution approach?
questions.a: The chapter says the limits of the Green Revolution have become visible over the last few decades, including long-term impoverishment of the soil and depletion of groundwater. It also says production of wheat and rice rose significantly, so the other explanations contradict it.
o: Its limits appear over decades: poorer soil, falling groundwater
Its methods fail at once, as they never raise wheat or rice output
Its seeds resist pests, so any loss is the weather's doing
Its machines cannot be used on any farm, so yields must fall

questions.q: A speaker says, 'Traditional farming has nothing scientific in it, so modern science has nothing to learn from it.' Show from the chapter why this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter reports that over 85 per cent of the practices were validated by modern science and could be applied to reduce chemical use and improve soil health. Neem-based pesticides and beejamrit show traditional ideas turned into modern solutions.
s: Cites the ICAR validation
Says they can reduce chemicals and improve soil health
Gives an example such as neem-based pesticides or beejamrit

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Hydroponics grows plants in nutrient-rich water solutions, giving the essential minerals directly to the roots.
2. Seeds from company-developed plants can always be sown again in the next season.
3. Sikkim, called the world's first 100 per cent organic state, banned chemical fertilisers and pesticides in 2014.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are from the chapter. 2 is false: 'always' is wrong, because the seeds are often not suitable for planting in the next season.
o: 1 and 3 only
3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: (a) Name two features that the chapter says traditional farming systems, such as kulagar and gokrishi, usually share. (b) Name one feature that tells the two apart.
questions.a: (a) They are usually aligned with natural cycles such as the cycle of seasons (ritu chakra), and often rely on family involvement and domestic animals. (b) Kulagar is a homestead system with many crops around the home in a structured irrigated design; gokrishi uses cows for manure and bullocks for ploughing.
s: (a) alignment with natural cycles and reliance on family and domestic animals
(b) a feature that separates them: kulagar's varied homestead crops or gokrishi's cows and bullocks

questions.q: A panchayat is split. Proposal 1: follow Sikkim and ban all chemical fertilisers and pesticides at once. Proposal 2: keep Green Revolution methods but add neem-based pesticides step by step. Evaluate the two proposals using the chapter's facts on Sikkim, on the productivity and the harm of chemicals, and on the trade-off between traditional and modern methods.
questions.a: Sikkim banned chemical fertilisers and pesticides in 2014, focused on natural farming and became the world's first 100 per cent organic state. Green Revolution methods are highly productive and can produce a substantial amount of food quickly, but chemicals pollute water, disrupt the ecosystem and harm bees, and the soil and groundwater suffer. Traditional methods are often more resilient and sustainable but may yield less. Neem-based pesticides are natural and much less harmful than chemical ones. The chapter says the challenge is to find a balance between modern innovation and the sustainable practices of ancestors, so a step-by-step plan or a full ban can each be defended, if the cost in food production and the gain for soil and water are weighed.
s: Sikkim's 2014 ban and organic model described
Productivity of Green Revolution methods against the harm of chemicals
Traditional methods more sustainable but may yield less
Neem-based pesticides as a natural option
A reasoned recommendation that balances food needs and sustainability

questions.q: Compare terrace farming, kulagar and gokrishi. Then analyse what the chapter says traditional farming systems usually have in common, and how traditional agriculture treats the plant and the soil.
questions.a: Terrace farming: steps cut into a hillside to give flat land, preventing erosion and conserving water. Kulagar: a homestead system in the Konkan with varied crops around the home in a structured irrigated design. Gokrishi: cows provide manure and bullocks plough the fields. Traditional farming systems are usually aligned with natural cycles such as the ritu chakra and often rely on family involvement and domestic animals. Traditional agriculture also treats the plant and the soil, with its whole ecosystem, as a complete system: soil organisms convert nutrients into forms plants can take up, and the plants support the organisms through their roots.
s: Terrace farming described
Kulagar described
Gokrishi described
Traditional systems aligned with natural cycles and relying on family and domestic animals
Plant and soil as one complete system, with soil organisms and roots

questions.q: A farmer wants to follow the chapter's sustainable pathways. Which one of these plans does NOT fit them?
questions.a: The chapter's sustainable pathways include organic farming with compost, seed cake and manure and natural neem-based pesticides. Chemical fertilisers are what organic farming avoids.
o: Replace compost with a heavier dose of chemical fertiliser to raise yield quickly
Spray a neem-based pesticide on the crop when pests appear
Use seed cake and animal manure as natural fertilisers on the field
Practise organic farming, avoiding chemical fertilisers and pesticides altogether

questions.q: A teacher summarises hydroponics for the class. Which of her sentences is NOT in agreement with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says hydroponics grows plants in nutrient-rich water solutions, giving essential minerals directly to the roots, in controlled environments, which makes it an option for urban farming and for areas with poor soil quality. It does not use soil.
o: Plants are grown in soil that is kept moist with nutrient-rich water
Plants are grown in nutrient-rich water solutions
Essential minerals are given directly to the roots
It is used in controlled environments, so it is an option for urban farming

questions.q: A state offers farmers electricity for irrigation at lower prices. Under which kind of help does the chapter place this, and what is it meant to lower?
questions.a: The chapter says the government provides electricity for irrigation at lower prices to reduce input costs. Crop insurance covers risk, purchase of crops helps marketing, and forecasts are information.
o: Support with costs: it is meant to reduce input costs
Support against risk: it is meant to repay crop losses
Support in marketing: it is meant to raise the price of the crop
Support with information: it is meant to give weather forecasts

questions.q:
Sarita farms 2 hectares of paddy. Cultivation costs ₹40,000 per hectare and the expected crop is worth ₹90,000 per hectare. Untimely heavy rain destroys 60 per cent of the crop. She had joined the government's Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana at a premium of ₹5,000 for the 2 hectares. Assume the scheme pays out ₹40,000 for such a loss.
(a) What kind of scheme is this, and what help does the chapter say it gives?
(b) What was the value of the crop destroyed?
(c) What is her net result, with and without insurance, after cultivation costs?
(d) A neighbour says the ₹5,000 premium is wasted in a good year, when the crop would earn her ₹1,00,000 after costs, so he will rely on a loan. Whose choice is wiser for a farmer like Sarita? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) A crop insurance scheme, giving financial assistance to farmers when the crop is lost, for example to untimely rain. (b) 60 per cent of ₹1,80,000 = ₹1,08,000. (c) Without insurance: 72,000 - 80,000 = -₹8,000. With insurance: -8,000 + 40,000 - 5,000 = ₹27,000. (d) A defended choice: insured, she turns a loss of ₹8,000 into a gain of ₹27,000 and avoids a loan that could lead to a debt trap; the neighbour saves ₹5,000 in good years and is acceptable only if he can bear a loss like this one.
s: Part (a): crop insurance, giving financial assistance for crop loss
Part (c): -₹8,000 without and ₹27,000 with insurance
Part (d): a decision weighing the premium against the loss and the debt trap

questions.q: The chapter gives the average landholding as about three-fourths of a hectare. Using the chapter's value of 1 hectare in square metres, this is about ___ square metres.

(a) Put these in the order in which the chapter describes them: farmers abandon agriculture; farmers take loans in hardship; the debt trap closes on them; repaying the loans proves difficult. (b) The chapter says as many as 2,300 farmers a day abandon agriculture 'according to some estimates'. At that rate, how many in 30 days, and why should the figure be quoted as an estimate?
questions.a: (a) Loans taken in hardship; repaying them is difficult; the debt trap; farmers abandon agriculture. (b) 2,300 x 30 = 69,000 farmers; the chapter gives the number as 'according to some estimates', so it is not an exact count.
s: (a) loans, difficulty repaying, debt trap, abandoning agriculture in that order
(b) 69,000, quoted as an estimate because the chapter says 'according to some estimates'

questions.q: True or False: A farming family with a 0.75-hectare plot that also keeps goats and poultry can still find, according to the chapter, that its total income does not give a decent quality of life.
questions.a: True. The chapter says families have traditionally had income beyond crops, which builds resilience, but today this is proving to be inadequate to provide a decent quality of life; farmers with small landholdings are not able to earn much income.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: other income sources build resilience but are now inadequate, and small holdings earn little

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many Indian farmers earn little from their land.
Reason (R): The average landholding is only about three-fourths of a hectare.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and a very small plot limits the produce and income, as the chapter says, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Two families each have a 0.75-hectare plot that earns ₹45,000 a year. Family X also earns ₹15,000 a year from goats and poultry; Family Y has no other income. (a) What share of Family X's total income comes from outside the crop? (b) Which family is better placed if the crop fails, and which sentence of the chapter says why?
questions.a: (a) 15,000 / 60,000 = 25 per cent. (b) Family X; 'Diversity builds resilience'.
s: (a) 25 per cent
(b) Family X, since diversity builds resilience

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Ganga basin has been a source of food and water to over 500 million people.
Reason (R): The Ganga river is under stress, and parts of it are not navigable in summer.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the river's stress is a present problem, not the reason the basin supports so many people, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A cooperative has funds for either a cold-storage unit for vegetables or a training day on new farming practices, but not both. The members' main complaint is that they must sell at whatever price traders offer at harvest. (a) Which would you choose, going by the chapter? (b) Give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) The cold-storage unit. (b) The chapter says promotion of cold storages (and better access to information and markets) enables farmers to get better prices for their produce, which addresses the complaint about prices; training helps with practices, not with the price at harvest.
s: (a) the cold-storage unit
(b) cold storages help farmers get better prices for their produce

questions.q: Farmers in a hill village sell tomatoes to the first trader who arrives, because they do not know the prices elsewhere. Which help from the chapter is meant to fix this?
questions.a: The chapter says better access to information and markets through the use of digital technology, along with cold storages, enables farmers to get better prices for their produce. The other supports lower costs, cover risk or supply inputs.
o: Information and market access through digital technology
Electricity for irrigation at lower prices for farmers
Crop insurance such as the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana
Supply of seeds, fertilisers and pesticides to farmers

questions.q: A village has 600 farming families who hold 450 hectares in all. (a) What is the average holding per family, and how does it compare with the average the chapter gives? (b) What difficulty with tractors does the chapter say such farmers face?
questions.a: (a) 450 / 600 = 0.75 hectare, the same as the average the chapter gives (about three-fourths of a hectare, the size of an average football field). (b) The machines are designed for larger farms and are expensive to buy or rent.
s: (a) 0.75 hectare, equal to the chapter's average
(b) tractors and machines are designed for larger farms and are expensive to buy or rent

questions.q: Four brothers inherit 3 hectares and divide it equally. How does each brother's share compare with the average landholding given in the chapter?
questions.a: 3 hectares among four is three-fourths of a hectare each, which is the average landholding in the chapter. Half, one and a half or double come from not dividing correctly.
o: It is equal to it
It is half of it
It is one and a half times it
It is double it

questions.q:
Thakur's family had 6 hectares. His three sons divided it equally. One son, Arun, later divided his share equally between his two children. A hectare of crops gives about ₹60,000 net a year. Arun's daughter Meenu keeps 15 goats and some poultry, earning ₹25,000 and ₹15,000 a year. A machine designed for small farms costs ₹1.2 lakh; it would save her about ₹12,000 a year in labour, and she could rent it to neighbours for about ₹18,000 a year.
(a) How many hectares does Meenu get, and how many square metres is that?
(b) Is Meenu's holding above or below the national average, and by how much?
(c) What are Meenu's yearly earnings from crops and from other sources together, and what share of this is from other sources?
(d) Meenu is thinking of buying the machine. Advise her.
questions.a: (a) Arun gets 6 / 3 = 2 hectares; Meenu gets 2 / 2 = 1 hectare, which is 10,000 square metres. (b) Above the average of three-fourths of a hectare by one-fourth of a hectare. (c) Crops ₹60,000 plus other sources ₹40,000 = ₹1,00,000; other sources are 40 per cent. (d) A reasoned decision: buying brings about ₹30,000 a year, so it pays back in about 4 years, and the chapter says machines for small farms now exist; but ₹1.2 lakh is more than a year of her total earnings and may mean a loan, which the chapter links to the debt trap. Renting a machine or adding more livestock income are alternatives.
s: Part (a): 1 hectare = 10,000 square metres
Part (b): above, by one-fourth of a hectare
Part (c): ₹1,00,000 with 40 per cent from other sources
Part (d): advice that weighs the machine's cost and payback against the loan risk

questions.q: A newspaper says, 'Dividing land among heirs does no harm, because each heir gets the same farm as the father.' A farmer has 3 hectares; he divides it equally among four children, and each of them later divides her share equally among three children. Show that the claim cannot be right and find the final holding in square metres.
questions.a: Each child gets 3 / 4 = 0.75 hectare, and each grandchild gets 0.75 / 3 = 0.25 hectare, which is 2,500 square metres. The holding shrinks at each division, which is the challenge of decreasing landholding.
s: Child's share 0.75 hectare
Grandchild's share 0.25 hectare = 2,500 square metres
Concludes that holdings shrink with each division

questions.q: Prakash and his neighbour Girish both lost their crop to untimely rain. Prakash borrowed money and is now deep in debt. Girish had crop insurance and borrowed little. Why is Girish less likely to fall into the debt trap, going by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says farmers can access financial assistance through crop insurance schemes such as the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, and that loans taken in hardship, which are hard to repay, lead to the debt trap. Assistance after a loss reduces the need to borrow. The other options claim things the chapter does not say.
o: Assistance for the destroyed crop means he does not have to borrow heavily
The scheme forgives every loan he has taken from anyone, whatever its source
The government buys back his destroyed crop at fair prices after the rain
Untimely rain does not affect insured fields, so no crop is lost

questions.q: Make up a short situation (three lines) in which a farm family faces two of the challenges in the chapter. Then suggest two ways in which the government or the family can respond.

questions.q: A village of small landholders has just lost much of its crop to untimely rain, and its produce is sold to traders at low prices. The panchayat can ask the government for only two of these: crop insurance, electricity for irrigation at lower prices, purchase of important crops at fair prices, and cold storage with digital access to markets. Choose two, justify your choice from the chapter, and say what the other two would do instead.
questions.a: A reasoned choice, for example crop insurance and purchase at fair prices. Crop insurance (such as the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana) gives financial assistance when untimely rain destroys the crop, which reduces the pull of loans and the debt trap. Government purchase of important crops ensures farmers have no difficulty marketing their produce and get fair prices, which meets the complaint about low prices. Cheaper electricity lowers input costs for irrigation and does not repay a loss; cold storage and digital access help farmers get better prices but need facilities set up. Other pairs, such as insurance with cold storage and digital markets, can be defended with the same facts.
s: Two helps chosen from the four
Insurance linked to the loss from untimely rain or to avoiding the debt trap
Purchase, cold storage or digital access linked to better prices
What the two helps not chosen would do instead (lower input costs; better prices through storage and information)
A justification that ties the choice to the village's two problems

questions.q: A student suggests, 'To help the farmers of the Ganga basin, divert even more river water to irrigation.' Evaluate this suggestion using what the chapter says about the basin: why it matters, the causes of its stress, and what may happen if the condition persists.
questions.a: The suggestion would worsen the problem. The basin has rich alluvial soil and has fed and watered over 500 million people. The chapter lists the causes of stress: Himalayan glaciers melting at an unprecedented rate, much water diverted to irrigation, huge amounts of groundwater pumped out by agriculture and industry, and hundreds of dams interfering with the flow. Diversion to irrigation is already one of the causes, so more diversion adds to the stress. If the condition persists, agriculture in the basin may become less sustainable, threatening the livelihoods of millions and India's food production. Efficient use of water would be a better direction.
s: Why the basin matters: rich alluvial soil, over 500 million people
Causes of stress named, including diversion for irrigation
Diversion for irrigation is itself a cause, so more diversion makes it worse
Possible effect: agriculture less sustainable, threatening livelihoods and food production
A better direction, such as efficient water use
